304191,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.6.2,1910-04-14,c1cd2cd5-6d25-4da0-9c10-9abb0e20f093,ca.m.7207,Mr. A. M. BEAUPARLANT (St, Hya-cinthe).",,QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.,,,"(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are proceeded with, I wish to give some explanations in order to dispel a misinterpretation prevailing in the public at large about the Bill I have laid before the House. Some newspapers have made remarks on that Bill concerning the seizure of the salary of the officers of parliament which I have introduced a short while ago. I would not have pointed out those remarks if some people had not persisted to make them repeatedly, falling into the same mistake and if that question did not concern to an enormous extent all the persons employed in the civil service I am bound therefore to set right that misrepresentation and to explain as matters stand.

I am not to take the time of the House to explain what are those mistakes. I will go straight to the point and say that this Bill is intended to make liable to seizure the salary of the officers of the federal government without distinction nor exception, from the ministers-if some of them have any debts-judges and members, to the last of the messengers. There is no distinction made. The intention is to reach the employees which have debts unpaid. The obligation of paying one's debts is a strict duty laid before everybody. I do not see why a federal servant should be more than any other citizen dispensed with that obligation.
The fairness require that everybody should be on an equal footing and it is an act of liberalism to replace a privilege by the parity of condition.

However, many of the public officers do not need the interference of the legislator to do honour to their engagements, but the number of those who neglect this duty is enough notable to justify the Bill.'

Some newspapers assert that not only a part, but the whole salary shall be liable to seizure. That is another mistake. A part only shall be liable to seizure. Indeed to seize the. whole salary of a heavily entangled servant should not be human. For such a man, having no more means of living, it should be better to resign. The intention of the Bill is to make only one part of the salary liable to seizure which is determined by the law of each province.
It is only the carrying our of the principle of seizability of salaries as regards civil servants as well as other debtors.

As I am pointing out the mistakes made by certain newspapers, allow me to recall the fact that the day after that on which I made my remarks on the Naval Bill, some newspapers credited me with having made statements which I never made. No remarks of mine, either in the French or English version of the ' Hansard,' whether in the revised or unrevised edition, justify them in stating that I ever made such assertions. In fact, these errors have not been made in bad faith and may be explained by the fact that the press reporters are not always near enough to hear distinctly the utterances of the member who is speaking.

One third and last point fn regard to which a plea of good faith can not be maintained is the following: A certain Quebec newspaper has a good deal to say about me. It is true that two or three years ago, I had the misfortune, which it considers as a very evil deed on my part, to have it condemned for libel.

,Liberal,,Aimé Majorique Beauparlant,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=c1cd2cd5-6d25-4da0-9c10-9abb0e20f093&Language=E&Section=ALL

304200,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.9.1,1910-04-14,26ad1170-885a-462b-b4fe-d5b28a33f671,ca.m.8518,Mr. BOYCE.,,RELEASE OF TWO PRISONERS.,,,I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to an article in the issue of the Canadian Municipal Journal and Telephone Building News for April, as follows :
WHERE WAS THE PULL?

Two months ago Judge Winchester, Toronto, sentenced L. J. Skellie and J. G. King to one year's imprisonment in the Central Prison for distributing obscene literature and post cards. The judge spoke vefy severely in giving the sentence, saying that if the youth of this country was to grow up in the right way, scoundrels who acted as the prisoners had done must be severely punished. Both prisoners pleaded guilty, and two stenographers gave evidence that they have refused to work for the prisoners, so filthy was the business.
Needless to say, the sentence of Judge Winchester gave great satisfaction.
On the 4th of March, these two prisoners, after serving only two months-or one-sixth -of their sentence, were released with an absolutely free pardon by the order of the Minister of Justice .
The question that is now being asked is,
' where is the pull ?'
Mr. Robinette, K.C., defended the prisoners -though it seems strange that an eminent lawyer should stoop to such a dirty case- and he, it is understood, is a personal friend of the minister.

Some of the few fearless members of the House of Commons should ask the minister on what grounds he set aside the decision of such a careful judge as Judge Winchester; and how he considers it consistent with the justice, for the department to let loose two such offenders.

Such an action is not only a blot on the administration of justice-for if the minister is right, Judge Winchester is wrong-but it is a tremendous discouragement to those who are charged with catching criminals; the police. What on earth is the good of a line police force, such as that of Toronto, when their successful efforts to trace, arrest and secure the conviction of a public nuisance is set aside by the head of the Department of Justice?

The whole thing is a pure farce. If the Minister of Justice condoned dealing in obscene literature, let him secure an amendment to the Criminal Code, so that the public and the police may know that it is legal in Canada.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Arthur Cyril Boyce,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=26ad1170-885a-462b-b4fe-d5b28a33f671&Language=E&Section=ALL
304201,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.9.2,1910-04-14,f086f57f-8342-4b2e-819a-37713991d665,ca.m.6610,Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH.,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,RELEASE OF TWO PRISONERS.,,,I have a fairly accurate memory of the circumstances of the case to which the hon. gentleman has referred but the matter is one of considerable importance and I would therefore prefer, before making any statement in regard to it, to refer again to the file in order that I may not, by possibility, make any slip in stating the facts of the case. But I want to take this earliest possible opportunity to deny and to repudiate with whatever indignation and resentment I am capable of, the absurd and utterly untrue insinuation of the article in question that the gentleman named in the article, Mr. Robinette of Toronto, or any other man has the slightest influence or pull, as it is called, with the Department of Justice in connection with applications of this character. My memory is, and 1 think I am not mistaken, that in this particular case Mr. Robinette did not figure in any way whatever. I am certain that the solicitor who represented the principal defendant, a man named Skill, not Skelly, was of the opposite political party to Mr. Robinette and so far as I can now recall Mr. Robinette had no connection whatever with either of the prisoners nor did his name appear in any way in connection with the application. Certainly he never saw me in connection with the matter and if he had anything to do with it it was limited to the writing of a letter or something of that character. I stated when I rose I should prefer not going into the circumstances in the case upon this occasion, but with the permission of the House I would like to take an early opportunity to do so, because although I deprecate, as on previous occasions I have repeatedly deprecated, a public discussion

in this House or elsewhere of the action which, in the exercise of his prerogative and under the advice of his minister, His Excellency takes in matters of this character, this particular case is one, especially in view of the canards which the hon. gentleman has brought to the attention of the House, in which I think it would be well that the facts should be known to the public.

,Liberal,,Allen Bristol Aylesworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f086f57f-8342-4b2e-819a-37713991d665&Language=E&Section=ALL

304206,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.11.1.1,1910-04-14,,,,stagedirection,,,,Richard Blain, the Conservative member for Peel, and one of the whips for Ontario, was exposed in the House of Commons wes-terday as being on a patronage list of the government. It was all his own doing, at that. If he had kept quiet nobody would have known anything about his private dealings with the government, but the fatal blow came at about 5 o'clock.
The House was in Committee of Supply on a Post Office Department vote of more than $500,000.
Mr. Blain, as usual, began harping on the question of patronage, and incidently asked the Postmaster General if he had a patronage list in his department.

' So far as I am aware,' replied Mr. Le-mieux, ' there is no patronage list in my department. But I remember the member for Peel coming to me once and asking for a post office in some part of his county. And I think I granted him his request and built the post office for him.'
' Then,' cried Hon. Wm. Pugsley, Minister of Public Works, in evident glee, ' the member for Peel is on the patronage list.'
' Oh, yes,' answered Mr. Lemieux, ' he's on the patronage list.'
Mr. Blain could not withdraw, and had to admit that he was guilty of accepting patronage from the other side of the House.
I think I may say this is the first time I ever directed the attention of the House to any newspaper criticism of myself, but I thought this was so villainous that 1 would not allow it to pass.",,,,
304207,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.11.2,1910-04-14,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,,TORY WHIP ON PATRONAGE LIST.,,,"Don't you mean humorous instead of villainous?

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
304208,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.11.3,1910-04-14,96798f2e-2759-407e-8682-bc91559c9f45,ca.m.1056,Mr. BLAIN.,,TORY WHIP ON PATRONAGE LIST.,,,I see the humorous side of it, too. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I never at any time, either publicly or privately, made a request to the government for a post office to be erected in the county of Peel, I make that statement without fear of contradiction. I did ask on two occasions that a post office be opened at a very small village, not a village, but at the junc-

tion of two cross roads in my county, and I am frank when I say that my hon. friend the Postmaster General acceded to my request, and two post offices were opened up, But never a dollar was expended in the county of Peel by any department of this government since I have had the honour of representing it in the way of public works. I say this because it is unfair that I should be charged with asking the government for a post office that I know they would not build.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Blain,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=96798f2e-2759-407e-8682-bc91559c9f45&Language=E&Section=ALL

What I want to say is. that the government of this country is charged with the responsibility of adminstering its affairs in the best interests of the people, and the responsibility for that administration does not rest upon the individual here or there who may be most intimately concerned. In administering Indian affairs, whenever and wherever the Indians are holding land which they are not using for their own benefit, or which they are occupying to their own detriment, because of its geographical or other situation, and wherever such land may be turned into money which would be of more benefit to the Indians than the land, then it is the policy of the government to secure the surrender of the land by the Indians and the exchange of that land into money that would be for the benefit of the Indians, and to change the condition of that land from lying dormant and useless under the ownership of the Indians to that of productive and tax-paying land under the ownership of white people who are willing to pay a fair market price for it. I hope I have succeeded in making the policy of the government on that question clear. I want to impress upon the House that in so far as I understood the hon. gentleman, and in so far as I understood him to be supported by his friends on the other side of the House, they were against that policy.

304239,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.14.2.23,1910-04-14,intervention,,,,SUPPLY-ST. PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,The facts in regard to this case are all on the table of the House. My hon friend has asked for returns from time to time and every return that he has asked for has been laid on the table. If there is anything more that ne wants he should ask for it. Tf his case, as substantiated by the documents before the House, is not complete it is his fault and not ours. But the case is complete, he has asked for

everything and he has received it. Now, the documents on the table of the House show that the surrender of the lands of the Indians was the result and grew out of the attempt that was being made to secure the rights of whites and half-breeds who held lands individually within the area occupied by the reserve. There was no premeditation in regard to the surrender of the reserve.

May I give an explanation to the House as to the condition of this reserve so as to make it absolutely clear that what I state is the fact and so that the House may draw its own conclusions as to what my hon. friend stated. This reserve is situated on the Red river. The Red river, as the House knows, empties into Lake Winnipeg and the valley of the Red river, being very low, at the entrance of the river into Lake Winnipeg, there is a considerable area of what may be called debatable ground, land which, under certain circumstances, is dry and under other circumstances, wet. Sometimes it is an impassable marsh, and sometimes it is good hay land.

The northern limit of settlement along the valley of the Red river occurs within the limits of this reserve. Let me emphasize the point. The northern limit of settlement in {he valley of the Red river occurs within the limits of the St Peter's Indian reserve From the international boundary to this northern boundary of settlement, along both sides of the river when the transfer from the Hudson Bay Company to Canada occurred, the territory was occupied by settlers to the end of the arable country at the edge of the marsh which forms the southern end of Lake Winnipeg, and one of the first acts ol the Canadian government on taking possession of the country was to cause a survey to these lands in what was called the river settlement extending from the 49th parallel to Lake Winnipeg, and what afterwards became the St. Peter's Indian reserve was surveyed into river lots just the same as all the rest of the valley This was done because it was in the occupation of a settled population whose rights were exactly the same as of all the rest of the people who were settled ahum the Red river. After this river lot survey had been made, a certain portion of the people who occupied these river lots in what is now the reserve, decided that they would, as it is called there, enter the treaty. There was a very large admixture of Indian blood and as also of white blood in the people settled in that area, tout, the Indian blood I presume predominated, and as a result those occupants of these river lots, for one reason or another, whether owing to the predominance of Indian blood or for what other reason I am not here to

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,say, decided that they would enter the treaty and that this portion of the Red river valley surveyed into river settlements should be declared an Indian reserve. But although some of the people who were settled in that area wished to toe classed as Indians there were certain others who did not, who refused to surrender their citizenship and insisted on retaining their individual property as individuals and this they were allowed to do, while the so-called Indians, although they got the benefit of treaty payments, although they had the benefit of the presence of an agent, although in law they , were only Indians, still continued to occupy the same river lots, they and their families, until the recent arrangement was made with them. So that so far from these people toeing Indians in the ordinary sense of the word, or this being an Indian reserve in the ordinary sense of the word, the statement that this was the fact, if my hon. friend made it, was, as I said, an inexactitude. After these people had decided to be classed as Indians, being entitled under the Indian treaty to a larger area of land than was included in the river lots which they occupied, there was set apart as an Indian reserve for their benefit a certain surrounding area of land, making in all some 50,000 acres roughly speaking, which was placed under the jurisdiction of the Indian Department with an agent at Selkirk. This Indian reserve adjoined, either actually or approximately, the- town of Selkirk which had (been founded there, I think I am correct in saying, before this land was set apart as an Indian reserve.

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,Then my hon. friend and I are in agreement as to the proximity of the town and the reserve. I am glad to find a point of agreement in the remarks I made, although I was not able to find any such point in the remarks of my hon. friend. This area was set apart as an Indian reserve, with all the advantages and all the disabilities of such a reserve, and I need not point out to those members who are familiar with the conditions existing where there is an Indian reserve, near a town that that condition is not good either for the town of Selkirk, or for the Indians occupying the reserve. I need not go into details, every member who knows anything about the circumstances connected with an Indian reserve in proximity to a town knows the facts to be as I have stated. What made the matter worse, however, was that these river lots which had not become part of the Indian reserve, but which were occupied by people, either whites or halfbreeds, who claimed the rights of citizenship, w'ere included in that area, alternat-

ing with the lots that belonged to ordinary Indians, and the result was that there was no possibility of enforcing the liquor law in regard to Indians in that area, because intervening lots that belonged to white people or half-hreeds, were not under the Indian Act, and the fact that they were there, intermingled with the lots which belonged to the Indians, made it a simple, actual, physical impossibility to preserve law and order in all particulars upon that reserve, as it can be preserved on a reserve where there is no such intermingling of private property and band property. Whatever may be the claims of the Indians upon the consideration of the government, I suppose everybody will admit that the people who are not Indians are entitled to consideration, to claim the attention of the government, and so from time to time, from the setting apart of the reserve, complaint was made by citizens who held property within the reserve, who asked title to their property. I shall not take time to explain the conditions that surround the granting of title in such cases, I will only say that there were such difficulties, and that they occurred not in all cases, but in a very considerable number of the cases. From time to time the effort was made by the government of Canada, by commissioners sent there, to secure a settlement as between the Indian band and the individual holders of land within the limits of what is called the St. Peter's reserve. Up to a certain date some 5,000 acres of these private properties had been patented; but there still remained a number of claims that had not been settled, where private owners occupy river lots in the reserve claimed that they were entitled to patents, and the Indian band objected to the patents being granted. It was to secure a settlement of that condition of affairs, to secure the citizens of Canada who own the land within the limits of that reserve their legal title to their own land, that the commission in the person of Chief Justice Howell was appointed. Chief Justice Howell was asked to act as commissioner for the purpose of adjusting the claims of the white and halfbreed occupants of river lots in the St. Peter's reserve.

304258,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.14.2.42,1910-04-14,6e8d69a0-c443-4d32-9982-364df1473067,ca.m.2836,Mr. OLIVER.,Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs,SUPPLY-ST. PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,If my hon. friends can translate those words into an instruction, they are welcome to their interpretation. I

said that Chief Justice Howell was instructed to secure the rights of the citizens who held lands in the reserve. I gave it to be understood by the House that he had not been instructed to secure the surrender. The House has heard the instructions, and is the judge as to whether I stated what was correct or not. There is no hope, Mr. Speaker, of my hon. friend and myself understanding these things alike. I said at the beginning, in order to reach a conclusion let us have the records on the table of the House, and then we will know whether facts are as stated or not. In this case the fact was stated. It was challenged and the fact was proven from the records.

I say that when Chief Justice Howell, acting on his instructions, visited the reserve and attempted to make an arrangement that would protect the rights of the individual owners of property there, he found that it would be necessary, in order to reach a conclusion satisfactory to all parties, to secure the surrender from the Indians. Now, the charge of my hon. friend from Selkirk was that the department had deliberately planned to secure that surrender for the purpose of improperly benefiting their party friends. I have stated the facts as to how the negotiations came to be entered into, and I ask the House, is there a shadow ot foundation for the suggestion my hon. friend has made ? Does he suggest to this House that the hon. the Chief Justice of Manitoba, who was aum-orized to settle certain conflicting claims on the reserve, went on and negotiated the terms of a surrender upon the instructions of this government and with the view of advantaging the party friends of this government there? That is what my hon. friend insinuated in his address of last night. The facts that I have stated justify every word that I have used in regard to my hon. friend and his remarks. Here was a condition of affairs that required adjustment, required to be dealt with, in the interest of the town of Selkirk, in the interest of the Indians and in the interest of the private holders of land in the reserve; and Chief Justice Howell, having been appointed commissioner to settle one side of the question, went on and made negotiations that resulted in the settlement of the whole question. So far, therefore, as that insinuation of my hon. friend is concerned, I leave it to the House to judge what foundation he has for it.

In regard to granting land to the individual Indians in their own right, let me give the reason why that was done. These Indians were occupants of these lands in severalty at the time of the transfer. They did not become Indians in law until some years after the transfer. It is held, and the documents on the table will show how and to what extent it is held, that as residents of Manitoba in occupation of lands at that Mr. OLIVER.

time, they might reasonably claim consideration under the settlement that was made with the settlers of Manitoba of that date, in addition to their claims as Indians. That is to say, the claims which they held as Indians would not necessarily debar them from asserting claims for lands as original settlers in the province of Manitoba; and in order that that question might be settled, they were dealt with on the basis of giving out of this reserve 16 acres to each person in each family on condition that they signed away any rights they might have as original settlers in the province of Manitoba. It was for the purpose of quieting their title to land as original settlers that this arrangement was made with them, and it is so set out in the papers on the table and in the receipts for patents signed by all of those who received patents.
As t'o the providence or improvidence of this particular feature of the transaction,

I submit that in dealing with men who were individual owners of lands in 1871 and who were in individual occupation of that land down to the time of the negotiations for the surrender, it was not on the face of it an improvident transaction to place these men in individual ownership of that amount of land as a settlement of their title, not as Indians, but as white men or half-breeds. They had their rights as Indians, they were entitled to other rights as half-breeds, and it does not seem unreasonable that they should say: So far as our rights as Indians are concerned, the department shall administer them, but so far as our rights as half-breeds are concerned, we will administer them ourselves. That was_ the position of affairs. It was a condition of the surrender without which the surrender could not have been secured. It was considered by the commissioner who negotiated the surrender to be sound law and sound policy, and it was embodied in the terms of the surrender. Now, it is a fact that when the terms of the surrender were first drawn, a provision was made that the handling by the Indians of this land individually granted would be by the Department of Indian Affairs; but the people who were to sign the surrender, the people who owned the land, either as Indians or halfbreeds, were the people to say what terms were to be contained in the deed of surrender before they would sign it, and they said they would not sign it with that condition in it, and it had to be struck out.

As to the disposition that these people made of their lands after they had been granted to them, in a large number of cases they sold the land to whomsoever would buy at the price they were willing to take. I do not know what my hon friend or the other critics of the government in the House would have in regard to such a matter; but any assertion or insinuation that there was any pressure or

any possibility of pressure on the part of the government or any body connected with the government to compel one of these men to sell any portion of this land to any certain person or to take any certain price, is absolutely without foundation, as the records show.

,Liberal,,Frank Oliver,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6e8d69a0-c443-4d32-9982-364df1473067&Language=E&Section=ALL

Chief William Prince, the chief of the band who was said to have been bribed and 'bought and to have"" generally disgraced himself, and who at the same time might be supposed to be fairly sharp at making a bargain, sold 147-25 acres for $7.25 an acre. Alfred Spence sold two lots of land, one of 20 acres to the Northwest Land Company for $240, at the rate of $12 an acre, and one of 12 acres to F. Heap for $32, at the rate of $2.70 an acre.

It would seem to me that the figures I have read are evidence that the Indians to whom this land was given exercised their free right to dispose of it if they pleased, as they pleased, to whom they pleased, and at whatever price they pleased to take.

In view of the assertions that had been made, in view of the rumours that had come to me in regard to improprieties in the transactions between the people who had bought t'he lands and the Indians, contrary again to what my hon. friend suggested last night, as I told the House I contemplated doing, I sent the law clerk of the department to Selkirk with instructions to see the Indians who had sold land, and to find out whether they had been paid or not, the rumour being that they had not been paid, and that they were 'being cheated out of the money they were entitled to receive at the price at which they had sold. I told the House at the time the matter was in question that the government did not pretend to control the Indian in the price at which he sold the land or the person to whom he sold, that was a part of his right under the surrender; but as to whether he was getting the payment for it

or not, that was a matter that we might very well consider, and 1 proposed to consider it, although 1 did not hold the department responsible lor the price at which the Indian sold or the person to whom he sold. The law clerk was sent there, and 1 have placed on the table his report from which I read. In that report will he found the name of every Indian to whom land was given and the disposition that was made of the land. My hon. friend had that report in his hand, he knew that the lands which I have mentioned had been sold at the prices I have given, hut he saw fit last night in discussing this matter before the House to create the impression that the land had been sold at a price of some $4 an acre, without exceptions such as this, exceptions which absolutely prove that the Indian had the free right of sale and that he' got value for what he had to sell.

In regard to the taking of the surrender, my hon. friend was strong on the point that there had not been a sufficient advertisement or notice that the surrender was about to be asked. It is a fact which the records will bear out that the negotiations in regard to the surrender were in progress for the greater part of a year at intervals. Every Indian on the reserve knew that these negotiations were in progress. There are no people in the world who gather news quite as quickly as the Indians, especially news of direct interest to themselves, and there is no manner of doubt that they all knew and discussed the terms that were proposed, and that when Mr. Pedley went there on the completion of the negotiations, or the presumed completion of the negotiations by Chief Justice Howell, to take the formal surrender, the Indians thoroughly knew what proposition was being put before them and had their minds made up as to whether they would agree to it or not. My hon. friend said last night that only one day's notice was given for the gathering of the band. My information in that regard, as I am sorry to say in so many other matters, is quite different, it is that some three or four day's notice was given, and that there was an attendance of the band at the surrender of 205, out of a possible 289. It seems to me that the proportion of voting members of the band in attendance is ample evidence that ample notice was given, and that those who were not there were absent not because they did not know but because they did not care to be there. It is true that the surrender was carried by onlv a small majority: the vote, I am informed, was 107 to 98. But it *was a majority of thp voting members of the band who were present there, and the Indian Act recognizes that a surrender agreed to bv a majority of the voting members of thp band is a lerral surrender.

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,As I understand the law, they would have the legal right, but I would not consider they had the equitable right. But 1 do think that under the law, when there are 205 out of 289 present, they have not only the legal but the equitable right to decide, especially when it is a matter which had been under discussion for so long a time. As to the actual moment of taking the vote, as to what was done then, or how it was done, my hon. friend admits there was a fair division between the people who were voting for and against, those who stood on one side and those who stood on the other side. His suggestion that they did not know what they were voting on, is not worthy even of himself or of the Indians. They knew perfectly well. After a matter has been under discussion by them for a whole year, and they are asked to come and vote on a question, I say it is an insult even to an Indian to suggest that he does not know what he is doing or why he is doing it. From my acquaintance of the Indians, I think there are no people in the world who are quicker to appreciate their own side of the question than the Indians. So I say that the surrender was secured in a legal form, after due notice, in presence of a sufficient number of members of the band to constitute an equitable as well as a legal right. I say it would not be proper, it would not be sound policy in any sense, if, when it was absolutely in the interest of the public, absolutelv in the interest of the Indians, and absolutely in the interest of the surrounding settlements and of the settler within the limits of the reserve, that this settlement should not take place, that it should not be accepted and acceded to when a clear majority of those present voted for it.

The reason that we advertise school lands in June and July, or in the summer time, is because the school lands are scattered far and wide in the purely agricultural country, and it is neces-

sary for people to travel to see wliat the land is like, whereas, in this case, the land was situated within twenty miles of Winnipeg, it was land that anybody, who was at all likely to purchase, that is the people of Winnipeg and Selkirk, had no doubt made themselves familiar with in due course, knowing that it was going to be sold. In regard to the school lands it may not be out of place to inform my hon. friend that we held several school land sales on June 10, 1909, the lands being situated largely in townships 12, 13, 14 and 15, ranges 6 and 7, east of the 1st meridian; that is to say in the Selkirk area of Manitoba, east of the Red river, and in a northerly and easterly part of the province. With the favourable terms that are accorded school lands, under the satisfactory advertising that is given school lands, under all the favourable circumstances that go with the sale of school lands, these school lands in that part of the country only brought $5 an acre. This sale was in June, 1909, a year and a half after the sale of the reserve lands, after there had been a season of great prosperity, and at the beginning of a season which turned out to be even more prosperous, and still we were only able to secure the same average price for these lands that we secured for the lands in the Selkirk reserve.

It may be worth while taking the time required to place before the House the actual terms of this surrender so that there shall be no question about what its terms were. The document is as follows:
Know all men by these presents:

That we, the undersigned chief and principal men of the hand of Chippewa and Saul-teaux and Cree Indians, owning and resident on our reserve at St. Peter's, in the province of Manitoba, and Dominion of Canada, for and acting on behalf of the whole people of our said band in council assembled, do hereby release, remise, surrender, quit claim and yield up unto our Sovereign Lord the King, his heirs and successors forever, all and singular, that certain parcel or tract of land and premises, situate, lying and being in the county of Selkirk and province of Manitoba, containing by admeasurement 48,000 acres, be the same more or less, and being composed of the whole of the St. Peter's Indian reserve.

To have and to hold the same unto His said Majesty the King, his heirs and successors forever, in trust to dispose of the same to such person or persons, upon such terms as the government of Canada may deem most conducive to our welfare and that of our people, and upon the further condition that all moneys received from the sale thereof shall, after deducting the usual proportion for expenses of management, be paid as follows: one-half of said sum so remaining to be paid to us the year following the receipt of same by the government after sale of such lands, the balance of said proceeds of sale to be funded for our benefit and the interest paid

to us annually. At each payment as aforesaid the sum so paid shall he divided so that the chief shall receive each year the sum of $10 and each councillor the sum of $6 more than that to which the individual members of the band shall be entitled.

And upon the further conditions that out of the said St. Peter's reserve now surrendered there shall be granted an area not exceeding 21,000 acres to the members of the band as follows: to the chief 180 acres, to the ex-ehief and each councillor 120 acres, and to the other members of the band in the proportion of about 80 acres to each head of a family of five; grants to be made also in similar proportion to widows and to unmarried men and women over twenty-one years of age. A list of those entitled to grants and the patents thereof, and the area covered by each, as indicated in the above proportions, shall be made by the chief and councillors and a representative of the Department of Indian Affairs. The list shall be signed by the chief and councillors and by the Indian Department representative, and shall be the final settlement of the land to be patented, and of the parties to receive the same. In addition to the said 21,000 acres above mentioned there shall be set aside 3,000 acres of hay land for the members of the band having land in the present reserve or entitled to receive land under this agreement, it being understood that the Department of Indian Affairs mav from time to time reduce the quantity of hay land as the patentees sell the land so granted, and any land so taken off the land set aside for haying purposes shall be disposed of by the department for the benefit of the band.
A new reserve for this band shall be selected on Lake Winnipeg to the extent of 75,000 acres of available land, but shall not include more than ten miles water frontage.

The department is to make necessary survey of the lands to be patented and the lands sold as soon as expedient after surrender, and the patents to issue upon application of the individual Indian after the land is selected and properly designated.
My hon. friend from North Grey asked why we did not give the same length of time in selling these lands as in selling school lands. I have read him the answer.
The department shall advance at the time of surrender the sum of $5,000 to be repaid out of the first moneys received from the sale of the lands.
The treaty payments now made shall be continued, and also the yearly rations at treaty time.
A reasonable supply of agricultural implements and tools for use on the new reserve shall be supplied and distributed at the discretion of the department.
The department is to render reasonable assistance in removing to the new reserve in summer time in any year within five years of the date of this surrender.
Reasonable assistance in building on the new reserve shall be rendered by and at the discretion of the department; but any assistance so given is to be once and for all.
This surrender shall release lands in the present reserve from all claims of the band and of each individual member thereof from

all or any claims under the Manitoba Act or the Indian Act, and each member of the band shall sign a release to this effect when he receives his patent. Provided that such release shall not operate to exclude the band or any member thereof from participation in the proceeds or benefits of any lands held or disposed of by the government under the provisions of this surrender or according to law.

In the event of the representative of the Indian Department and the representatives of the band failing to agree upon the list of the lands to be patented, the matter will be referred to one of the .judges of the eastern judicial district of Manitoba, whose decision shall be final and binding on all parties.

And we, the said chief and principal men of the said bands of Chippewa and Salteaux Indians do on behalf of our people and for ourselves, thereby ratify and confirm, and promise to ratify and confirm, whatever the said government may do, or cause to be lawfully done, in connection with the said lands and this surrender.
In witness whereof, we have hereunto set our hands and affixed our seals this 24th day of September, in the year of Our Lord one thousand nine hundred and seven.

W. H. PRINCE,
His
JOHN X PRINCE,
mark.

JAMES X WILLIAMS,

John Semmons,
O. J. Grain,
Ernest Rayner.

All I am trying to make clear is that what was done was not the result of a conspiracy, as my hon. friend has suggested, but the result of consideration by officers of the government who could not possibly, under any circumstances, have had any interest or object in making such a report unless it was in the best interests of the country and of the Indians according to their belief and judgment.

Might I trouble the House for a few minutes to give a few words contained in the report of Chief Justice Howell on this transaction, first, to show the necessity for the surrender which was secured, and for the removal of the Indians in their own interests. He says:
The evidence of Mr. Vaughan-
That is the surveyor who made the first survey of the settlement in 1874.

-shows that at the time of his survey the people of this Indian settlement were then quite thrifty, the most of them could speak English, they were largely crossed with white; they had horses, cattfe and poultry; their houses were well built, better even than now, and their homes were those of whitemen rather than Indians. His map shows the houses by black dots, and the pink colouring shows the extent of ground then cultivated.

The evidence was that these people were retrograding instead of advancing, and the belief was that it was because of their situation, and that their own interest required that they should surrender their lands and be transferred to another location. Further on Judge Howell says:
Early in the investigation these claims-
That is of the Indians:
-and matters were brought before me. Out of about 50,000 acres, which remains of the reserve after deducting the area already patented, not more than 250 acres are cultivated.

Out of 48,000 or 50,000 acres only 250 acres were cultivated after an occupation in severalty 'by these people from 1874 to 1906. Surely that was a condition that called for some effort on the part of a government that had some regard for the interests of the Indians, and the progress of the country. It goes on to say:

Without (giving further reasons for my urging the surrender and without further description of the negotiations I can only say that they were the best I could get. Best for the government and best for the Indians, and without any hesitation I recommend the carrying out of the same.

That is to say the Chief Justice of Manitoba, who took a deep personal interest in this matter, and who had been familiar with it by reason of long residence in Manitoba, places himself on record as recommending this transfer as being the best that could be secured. It is true that Chief Justice Howell did not carry it out. My hon. friend laid great stress last night upon that fact. Truly, the surrender had actually, in form, to be conducted by the proper officer of the department, but Chief Justice Howell takes the full responsibility for the terms of the surrender in the words I have read, and I do not know where I could go, as minister of the department, to get better information or advice or more impartial or intelligent treatment of this question than to the gentlemen who penned that report. He says:
The new reserve is accepted by the band in full satisfaction of all damages claimed and of all rights, individual or tribal, asserted as above set forth:

It might not be improper for me to add that in my view of the matter the government by granting a new reserve of 75,009 acres have readily and cheaply got out of a nasty tangle and have greatly benefited the band, and have taken a step which in the near future will relieve the locality of an undesirable element, to say the least.

. I might mention that in the area of the reserve the number of claims occupied by people who were not Indians was 30 on the river lots, and one in the township survey with an approximate population of 157. It was the rights of these people that were the first consideration of the government in sending the commission. The transaction with the Indians by which the surrender was secured was an after, subsequent and subsidiary consideration, but as it turned out, was necessary in carrying out the first idea that we had and was generally to the benefit of all concerned.

My hon. friend drew attention last night to the fact that some of this land which had been sold at $5 an acre has since been sold at $50 an acre, and he asks the House and the country to believe that the government has in some way damaged either the Indians or the country by its course, of which this is the result. I am here to claim that it is a justification of the government, and an endorsement of their policy in securing the surrender.

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,Williams; and in sending a man of that ability and position, whose connection with the department was quite recent, and who could not be considered to be associated in any shape or manner with this transaction, we surely were doing everything that could be done to get any difficulties that might have arisen between

the Indians and the buyers settled on a fair basis; and, as a matter of fact, we have placed on the table of the House a report which states in detail what has become of every parcel of land that has been handed over-to whom it has been sold-the price paid for it, whether there have been any complaints or not with regard to the sale and everything about it; and any care that may be taken in looking over this list will demonstrate that the matter has been closed up satisfactorily to all concerned. However, it is not a matter that is free from difficulty. As an illustration, I will just mention a case of one of my hon. friend's particular friends, one of the Asham family-not the budding John Nor-quay, but possibly his brother or his son James Asham, No. 8 in the band. He had a general complaint about the surrender and the low price the Indians got for their land. Our report says that he sold 88 acres, that is, the whole of his right in severalty, to the Northwest Land Company for $449; but, believing that the price was too low, he sold 40 acres again to George Tracy for $160. He sold another 40 acres, or the same, I am not sure which, for a yoke of oxen. When I give the House this information, they will understand the difficulty that necessarily surrounds these transactions with the Indians, and the difficulty of getting them straightened up to the satisfaction of the Indians, and will know at what value to place the numerous affidavits, principally from the Asham family, -which my hon. friend brought to the attention of the House.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I have replied to every insinuation that my hon. friend made during his four or five hours speech; but I shall be glad to deal with any others that he or any other member may bring to my attention; because, as I said before, as I followed his address, he did not, in the whole four hours of its duration, make a single statement or insinuation with which I could agree or which to my mind was borne out by the documents on the table of the House.

If I may, I will try to give a short statement of the ease from our point of view. In pursuance of our policy of administering Indian lands for the benefit of the Indians and for the development of the country, we entered upon the effort to secure the surrender of this reserve. It was in peculiar circumstances in the many ways which I have detailed to the House. It was not an ordinary reserve; the circumstances were extraordinary in many particulars, and, therefore, extraordinary measures had to be taken in connection with the surrender. But so that these measures should be beyond question, the highest authority that could be got in the province of Manitoba was engaged to do the work. The attempt was successful. The

Indians have received their land in severalty; they have received a large sum of money as the result of the sale of land that was surrendered; they will have the marsh land to be sold as it comes into value; they have received a new reserve, very much better suited to, the particular life of the Indians, of 75,060 acres in area; they have received assistance at the hands of the department to remove to that reserve and to establish themselves upon it. As a result, the Indians have benefited. Instead of their having lost anything by the transaction, they have gained very greatly; and the only criticism of the arrangement that can be made, from my point of view, is that they were too liberally dealt with, that they got more than the country could afford to give to another band. But, as I say, the circumstances were exceptional, and the public interest and the interest of the Indians were so benefited in securing the surrender that the circumstances and the conditions are, in my humble judgment, justified and more than justified.

304365,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.14.2.149,1910-04-14,d970d184-d56d-4589-860d-306da0296ebf,ca.m.6096,Mr. W. S. MIDDLEBRO (North Grey).,,SUPPLY-ST. PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,I do not intend to tollow ad seriatim the statements made hy the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), bnt I propose to deal with them as I proceed with my argument. Before going farther, however, I cannot let the occasion pass without saying that I find it impossible to understand the proposition that when an hon. member on this side makes charges of malfeasance in any department of the government, there is no duty whatever devolving upon the government to investigate that charge unless, in the opinion of the minister directly responsible, he believes there is some foundation for it. If that proposition be true, no government would grant a commission to investigate into any charge unless the minister were willing to admit that he believed the charge made was well founded. But my hon. friend himself (Mr. Oliver) contravened that principle for he has in-formeu us that, in consequence of the statements made by the hon. member for Selkirk, he himself appointed a commission to investigate into some of the charges made. The very appointment of that commission, the sending of Mr. Swinborn and Mr. Williams there to make an investigation, is an admission that, in the minister's opinion, there is some truth in the allegations of my hon. friend. The doctrine I would lay down is that when a charge is made by an hon. member of this House, especially when that charge is backed up by some 25 or 26 statutory declarations, it is the duty of the minister, whose department is implicated, to make some kind of an investigation, because, if a prima facie case has been made out, the country is entitled to know whether or not there is anything in the charges made. As a general proposition-and if the hon. minister does not think it right, I would ask him to express his dissent-I say that the government are acting in all these matters affecting the Indians as their trustees and protectors. The poor Indian has been unwittingly and unwillingly placed in that position by reason of the march of white civilization. He is in that position against his will; and because we have placed him in that unfortunate position, and because we cannot expect of him those business characteristics which are foreign to his nature and training, we are obliged to protect him. And having assumed that guardianship, the government cannot contract itself out of the natural relations existing between the guardian and his ward. If the hon. minister dissents from that proposition, I would ask him to say so, because my argument is going to be based on it. If by any means you like, if by bringing a satchel before the Indians with $5,000 of money into it, and the temptation thereby created, or by any other means, you get them to consent to a transaction which is Mr. OLIVER.
not in their interests, you are committing a breach of your duty as guardian towards your ward.

Approaching the subject from that standpoint, I start- out with ascertaining what the land in question is worth. If it be worth only $5 per acre, the case against the government falls to the ground, so far as the financial interests of the Indians are concerned, but how do you judge the value of land? Will any one say that lands on this Indian reserve, situated within 25 miles of Winnipeg, on a branch line of the Canadian Pacific railway, because Selkirk is on a branch of that railway, with an electric railway from Winnipeg to Selkrk, do not occupy the first position in the province of Manitoba, so far as situation is concerned? Situation is the first consideration in determining the value of land; the second is the character of the soil itself. If you get good situation and good soil, as you do in this instance, you must admit that this St. Peter's reserve is the best land in the province of Manitoba. What evidence have I of that? I shall not ask the hon. minister to accept my statement, but I will take the records of the department itself. Those records were under the hands of the minister, and if he had given this case proper consideration, he could have, just as well as hon. members on this side, put himself in possession of that information; and if he had, he would not be here to-day ratifying and supporting a transaction which is a disgrace to the administration of his department.
Take the reports from his own agents on the very land in question. Here is the report of Inspector E. McColl, made in July, 1902:

Rich in black alluvial soil of the Red River valley, and extending through a fringe of poplar, ash leaf maple and elm. back to the prairies and hay lands. St. Peter's reserve is an ideal place for mixed farming.

Let me take the next year, The report for 1903 of the Indian agent for the same reserve, who happens to be Mr. John Sem-mons, the same man who was given such an excellent character by the hon. minister a few minutes ago. He says:

St. Peter's has an area of eighty square miles. All of these reserves are situated in areas of excellent land, suitable for farming and stock raising purposes, while at the same time they are adjacent to the water, and the natives may enjoy all the advantage of sailing and fishing. All conditions appear to contribute to the welfare and happiness of the people. . . . Some of the best soil in Manitoba is to be found in St. Peter's. All this is protected bv a fringe of wood to the west and northward. There is no reason why ten thousand bushels of wheat should not be raised here.
I come to the next year, the report of Mr. Semmons again for 1904. He says:

St. Peter's reserve has some of the best land in the province of Manitoba. It has the advantage of being very near to an excellent market. It also has the best shelter from north and west winds offered to any locality. lt_ is safe to say that properly cultivated it might produce one hundred thousand bushels of best wheat per year.

For 1905 there is no report, but for 1906, and this is the year the government issued a commission for the purpose of securing the surrender of the reserve, Mr. J. O. Lewis, Indian land agent, reports as follows:

St. Peter's reserve lies along the Red river, extending back 4 miles on each side, has a frontage of about 12 miles on the river. The inner two miles is divided into lots varying in width, &c. The land is a loam with a clay subsoil.

These evidences as to the value of the land were extracted from the records of the department and were just as available to the minister as to any member in this House. I now come to Chief Justice Howell, who was sent out there at the request of the department. What does he say as to the value of the land? He says:
The reserve is, in the main, excellent farm [DOT]lands, and the adjoining lands are fairly *well settled and cultivated, and the town of Selkirk joins it at the south side.
Then I take information furnished by the assessor of the municipality of St. Andrews, and this information is in the department also.

This department itself, in the very year it issued a commission to Chief Justice Howell, fixed the value of lands in this reservation by the sale of some lands by the department to the municipality of St. Andrews adjoining this reserve and I ask the government if there could be any more conclusive proof as to the value which they then set upon these lands than the fact that they charged and received $20 an acre in 1906 for these very lands. They sold $813 worth of land which figures out at $20 an acre. Then take land immediately adjoining the reservation owned by Mr. Funk. The evidence as given by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) is that that land is now selling for from $40 to $60 an acre. Then we have the evidence of the assessor of the municipality of St. Andrews, who says that at the very time these lands were being sold, part of these very lands were within the municipality of Selkirk, and as such were assessed, on the basis of one third of their value, at $7 an acre. He explains how they were assessed at $7 and how all lands of that class are assessed at. one-third of their value, in accordance with a graded scheme adopted in that municipality making the value of the land $21. Then I take the letter from Mr. Hudson, a partner of the son of the Chief
Justice of Manitoba, a man thoroughly familiar with values in that locality. His letter to the department shows that he values these lands at from $20 to $25. He says:

The land which has been bought at $5 an acre, is worth in the neighbourhood of from $20 to $25 an acre. The Indians are quite incompetent to look after their own interests, and none of them can afford the money necessary to carry on lawsuits to retrieve their possessions.

The next evidence is the case of Swan Lake Indian lands. I discussed this with some reserve, because I conceive that the arguments of the Minister of the Interior when quoting the value of other lands without knowing where they were situated were wholly irrelevant.

Throughout this agency the Indians are tteadily progressing, their mode of living is improving and they are becoming less dependent on others for their livilihood-*

Now if it is upon the ground of intemperance that the minister says this band should be removed, here is a report of his own agent who says that the band is not intemperate. Now, as to the duty of the government to protect the Indian with respect to the patented lands. We all know that the Indian Act provides that even in the case of chattels the gov-Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
ernment shall protect the Indians. Section 57 of the Indian Act says:

No agent for the sale of Indian lands shall, within his division, directly or indirectly, except under an order of the Governor in Council, purchase any land which he is appointed to sell, or become proprietor of, or interested in any such land, during the time of his agency; and every such purchase, or interest sliall he void.

I do not say that that section technically applies to the case in question because these Indian lands were patented to the individual. Still, the principle is the same and there is the fiduciary character of the department and of the Indian agent as representing the department, and if I can prove that the Indian agent himself who had the confidence of these Indians because of the fiduciary relation in which he stood to them; if I can prove that he availed himself of his fiduciary character for the purpose of obtaining lands from these very Indians, I think the minister will agree with me that I have given sufficient proof to justify him in making an inquiry into the' acts' of that man. Section 42, for the purpose of carrying out this idea, provided:

No official, or employee connected with the inside, or outside service of the Department of Indian Affairs, and* no missionary _ m the employ of any religious denomination, or otherwise employed in mission work among the Indians, and no school teacher, on an Indian reserve, shall, without the special license in writing of the Superintendent General, trade with any Indian, or sell to him directly or indirectly, any goods or supplies, cattle or other animals.

That is an entire prohibition of anybody dealing with the Indian except through the intervention of the Indian agent. That places the Indian agent in a very confidential fiduciary relation to the Indian, which is a further reason why there should not be any dealing between the agent and the Indian. Carrying out that very idea, the department has issued regulations which say:

No band, or irregular band of Indians, and no Indians of any band or irregular band of Indians in the* provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, or Alberta, or in the Northwest Territories, may, without the consent of the Indian agent for the locality, sell, barter, exchange or give to any person, or persons whatsoever, any grain, or root crops, or any produce grown on any Indian reserve in the said provinces, or territories, or on any part of such reserve, and that any such sale, barter, exchange or gift shall be absolutely null and void unless the same be made with such consent:

If the department saw fit to make such a regulation for the protection of the In- . dian in the sale of root crops and other personal property, how much more was it their duty, when they placed in the hands

of the Indian the absolute sale of these lands, to guard him with restrictions so that he would not be taken advantage of 'by speculators? Let us see what Mr. Lewis, the Indian agent, himself says as to the capacity of these Indians. In his letter of the 5th of July, 1909, to the department he says:

As agent I have refrained from any interference in the bargaining, but as some of the Indians are old and illiterate, and called upon me to assist in the accounts afterwards, I have rendered what assistance 1 was able. While a large percentage of the St. Peter's Indians resent interference in their business, there is, I believe, a majority of them too illiterate and helpless to manage a real estate sale, especially where the payment of the land extended, as in most cases it did, over a period of one year, and was made by orders on stores, and with truck and small cash payments. The Indians sold only in small parcels, and at different prices, and not always to the same buyer. The Indian gave a statutory deed as soon as he sold, setting forth the price, and description of the land. He received a small payment down with the promise of the balance as soon as he was able to deliver the patent. The selling began as soon as the locating started. Thus a year elapsed between some of the sales, and the receiving of the patent. There was nothing expressed in the deeds as to future payments, in fact, as far as anything was set forth in the deed, the Indian was paid in full. He was dependent entirely upon the honour of the buyer for the fulfilment of the verbal contract. You can readily understand that the accounts extending over so long a period have become long and complicated.

Now, I propose to prove a sale to the [DOT] Indian agent himself by a widow who was illiterate, and another from a man who was 90 _ years of age. The Minister of Interior said in his speech of the 29bh of November, that if we could prove that the Indian agent had been trafficking in these lands, he would soon see whether or not the agent would he dismissed from the service. I have before me a certified copy of a deed, dated the 8th day of April, 1908, eight months before the patent was issued. It is from Flora Bella Wesley, widow, and is to the agent himself, James Oscar Lewis. The consideration purports to be $235, and the land 23-57 acres, so that the price was $10 an acre. The woman swears that she did not get $10 an acre, and that she thinks she did not get more than $5 an acre, and she got that part in cash and part in goods. 1 find that Inspector Swiftford made an inspection of this matter, and wrote to the department on the 22nd of November last, as follows:

It must be remembered that all the laud buyers used the chief and councillors of the band as interpreters and as agents to bring Indians to them to induce them, if possible, to sell their lands, and in return these interpreters or agents were rewarded with $5 or more for each transaction in which a transfer of land took place.
The price usually paid them for allotments was about $5 an acre.
The white man predominates in the interpreter and witness, W. D. Harper, and it is quite possible that he may be induced to remember evidence iu favour of the buyer.

The inspector himself intimates that the witnesses and the interpreters take advantage of the Indians because they are employed by speculators, and get $5 for every piece of land they sell. In this case I find that the grantor is illiterate, as she makes her mark. The witness to the deed is W. D. Harper, one of the councillors who got 120 acres of land, ten times as much as any of the other Indians, for consenting to the surrender, and one of the men, the inspector says, who got $5 for every sale they made. The agent took advantage of his position as agent to obtain from this widow a deed of land for a consideration which he knew was away under its value. The other case is that of a man 90 years of age, also illiterate, who made his mark instead of signing his name. His land was also sold to the agent. For 32 acres he was to get $10 an acre, or $320 in all. This was to be paid at the rate of $6 a month. He said that when he was paid for 20 months, or in all $120, the payments stopped. His Statement is corroborated by Mr. Swinford. In both of these cases the Indian agent was trafficking in land with persons who were illiterate, both of whom say they did not get the consideration that they expected and that was agreed to; and this is proved by the certified copy of the deed Obtained from the Land Titles Office. I leave these cases with the minister, to der cide whether some inquiry should not be made into them.
With regard to another point, section 89 of the Indian Act says:

With the exception of such sum not exceeding fifty per centum of the proceeds of any lands, and not exceeding ten per centum of the proceeds of any timber or other property, as is agreed at the time of the surrender to he paid to the members of the band interested therein, the Governor in Council may, subject to the provisions of this parliament, direct how and in what manner, and by whom, the moneys arising from the disposal of Indian lands, or of property held or to be held in trust for Indians, or timber on Indian lands or reserves, or from any other source for the benefit of the Indians, shall be invested from time to time, and how the payments or assistance to which the Indians are entitled shall be made or given.

In other words, the section says that in any -disposition of an Indian reserve you cannot give the Indian more than one half of the proceeds. I grant you that the minister can point to the use of the word ' land '.
With the exception of such sum not exceeding 50 per cent of the proceeds of that land.

I take the proceeds of the ' land ' to mean the proceeds of the ' reserve/ In other words the government is not entitled to hand over to the Indians, for his own absolute use and disposal, even if the government thought it advisable, more than one half of the proceeds of the reserve. But what did the government do here? It handed over 23,000 acres of land, and there you have remaining 25,000 acres to be disposed of. Some of that had been sold by public auction and some of that will no doubt be sold in the same way later on. But they agreed in the surrender that of the balance over and above what they are entitled to by patent the Indians are to get one half of the proceeds. Therefore, the Indian has got 23,000 acres in fee simple and is entitled to get half the proceeds of the remaining 25,000 acres. Therefore, according to the hon. minister, he gets 23,000 patented plus proceeds of 12,500 acres or 37,500 acres in all, out of a total of 48,000, in contravention of the section which says that the Indian is not entitled, even if the government think it advisable, to more than one half the proceeds of the sale of the reserve. I think that is a good argument against the legality of the sale.

Now we come to the sale by public auction of a further portion of this reserve amounting to 15,000 acres. In view of the indisputable evidence as to the value of the land which I have just given, the mere fact that these lands were sold at anything less than $20 an acre should be conclusive evidence that they were sold under value. Would it not have been better to have offered these lands for sale when they were not covered by snow? Why was it not advisable to extend the period of payment to ten years annual instalments just as the hon. minister has done with respect to school lands? The hon. minister has replied that one reason why he -would not give ten years for payment of these lands was that he wanted to close the transaction and get rid of the Indians from that locality.
