PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,I would expect to make a little out of it after ten years. Now. as regards the quality of this land, I went to the trouble to get a report on the land as to its exact character, and I have this information which I believe to be correct. I will read to the House the statement I have received:

Going down the Red river from Winnipeg one cannot but be struck with the appearance of the country. The banks are high and literally lined with small houses, surrounded by gardens, and the trees in the distance give the country a beautiful appearance. It looks to be most desirable laud. The same character of country continues from Winnipeg to about 8 miles between Selkirk and the reserve. But disenchantment begins as soon as one goes one-quarter to one-half a mile back from the river. The land along the river banks is high but recedes from the river. One mile from the river the land is low, swampy, covered with black poplar and willow, or is open marsh. These lands have never been in use only as hay lands. In the parish of St. Peter's these features are more pronounced. The reserve runs practically through two townships, viz., 11 and 15 in ranges 1, 5 and 6 east. The river lots take up about all of range 5 in township 11. The land in township 14, on the west side of the river, at the rear of the river lots, or as it is known in the ' outer two miles ' is, as I have said, swampy, no timber, the only wood growth is willow and poplar brush, and this is diversified by open swamps and hay land. The soil is a heavy clay, known in the west as 'gumbo.' There was scarcely any competition at the sale for the land. No one who knew it wanted it. On the east side of the river, in township 11, range 6. east, the country is open with some scrub, but it is stony and gravelly, so stony that one cannot drive through on the trail without a great deal of care. The river lots on the east side are all covered with black and white poplar and willow. Everything that would make firewood or could be used has been taken off, as it has furnished the wood for the town of Selkirk and the immediate neighbourhood for 60 years. In township 15, ranges 4, 5 and 6, range 5 is all a floating marsh, ranges 4 and 6

ere covered with white poplar, interspersed with willow and marshes. The soil is good, but generally low, so low that the provincial government about 14 years ago built, by permission of the Indian Department, two miles of corduroy road, for the use of the people who live adjoining the reserve in the Poplar Park district, two miles of corduroy In this beautiful reserve.

Now, so far as advertising is concerned, the land was advertised as every other Indian land has been advertised, and it was well advertised. The usual rule was followed, the rule which has been followed since 1894. The advertisement was 'inserted in the press according to the order in council of May 8, 1894, and December 12, 1896. the latter of which says:

Advertisements should not be inserted in any books, pamphlets or periodicals other than newspapers published weekly or more frequently, and all advertisements should be limited to the maximum of six insertions in daily or weekly papers.

The Minister of the Interior gave the House the names of the papers in which this advertisement was inserted. Besides those papers, there were a number of hand bills sent out. There were 200 slips mailed to the parties who applied for this land. There were one or two hundred hand bills put around the town of Selkirk. Now, the town of Selkirk is the fifth largest town in the province of Manitoba. It is from 22 to 24 miles from the city of Winnipeg. It is served by the Canadian Pacific railway on the west side, by the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway on the east side, which is about three miles from the centre of the town of West Selkirk. It is also served by an electric railway giving a splendid service between there and the city of Winnipeg. It is centrally located, it is easy of access, and anybody who wished to purchase would have been very little inconvenienced by going from his home in any part of Manitoba to the town of Selkirk. The sale was well attended. There were from 100 to 200 present, if my information is correct. I attended a sale of school lands at Arnaud, in the county of Provencher, that year, and some of that land was sold at $27 an acre. There were about 150 people present, which was considered a good turn out, and it was considered to be one of the best school land sales held in western Canada. But the remarkable feature of that sale, as compared with this sale, was that for the cheap lands the upset price was fixed at $5, and there was only one-quarter section sold at $5 an acre. People preferred land for which they paid $15, $20, $22, $26 and $27 per acre to cheap land. There was only one-quarter section of cheap land sold. Then, as to the point raised by the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) regarding the price of the land; it was pointed out

by the minister that it was the poorest land on this reserve that was sold by auction, and that it was the best land that was allotted to the Indians. As to the numbers that purchased, I understood the hon. member for Selkirk last night to say that there were about six, that it was a party deal from start to finish, and that a man who was a good Grit could get all the land he wanted, while the man who was a good Conservative was barred. That is not possible at a public auction. As my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior stated to-day, the number of those who purchased was 24. Who were some of those men and what are their politics, if politics must enter into this as politics have entered into it contrary to the statement of the hon. member for Selkirk that this was a non-political question? One of the purchasers of this land was Mr. G. H. Funk. I know Mr. Funk, he was at the' sale at Arnaud to which I have referred; he is a wealthy man, and he is straightforward, honest and fair in his dealings. He is doing what I would do myself if I had some of his resources. He is buying western land because he is going to make money out of it. He purchased land at the St. Peter's Indian reserve. When Mr. Funk purchased this land he did not know when the surrender was made. He read the advertisement, went to Selkirk and entered into competition with those and got the portion of the land for which he had bid. Another was the Hon. Abraham Funk, an ex-senator of the United States. He is also an investor in northwest land. These gentlemen are both Americans, one of whom lives on the other side, and one lives in Winnipeg. Another man who bought land to the extent, I understand of $35,000, was Mr. J. L. Hyland, a contractor, who takes contracts for the Canadian Northern Railway Company. As far as anybody knows he has no politics, and perhaps if he could be persuaded by the corporation for which he works its inclination would lean him to the Conservative side. Another was Capt. Pollock, who has been a resident of Selkirk for many years. I know that gentleman, and he is a Tory of the Tories. He had .iust as much right to buy land there as anybody else. Believing that he had such a right, and having the money, he purchased the land and nobody could prevent him from doing that. But he is not a Liberal. Mr. Finkleman, a merchant of Selkirk and a member of the executive of the Conservative Association of Selkirk, or he was up to a short time ago, was another. He entered, as he had a right to do, into open competition and bought the amount of land that he thought he had a right to buy. Mr. J. C. Simpson, Conservative and ex-member of the Manitoba legislature, was another who purchased land there. His brother is now a member Mr. MOLLOY.

of the local legislature of Manitoba. He is what might be termed a blue-blooded Tory, just as good a Tory as sits on the other side of the House, just as good a Tory as there is in Canada. He bought land, as he had a right to, and he paid for it, or he will pay for it. As far as the political end of it is concerned it was just the same as it is at any other public auction- the man who bid the highest price got the land regardless of his political affiliations.

As far as the ignorance of the Indian is concerned, we were led to believe last night that you could almost do what you liked with the poor Indian. That has not been the experience of the majority of people, as the Minister of the Interior stated. The Indian is just about as clever and cute, when it comes to a question of dollars and cents, as the ordinary white man. I believe that the hon. member for Selkirk said that he did not believe that there were twenty Indians on the reserve who could read and write. I make the statement that there are not twenty between the age of from ten to forty tnat cannot read and write. I am not going to be positive as to that, but I know that the missionaries, such as Mr. Semmons, have done all they could to promote the education of the indian. They have had every opportunity to do that. There are seven day schools on that reserve-South St. Peter's, North St. Peter's, East St. Peter's, Muckle's Creek school, Peguis' school, Roman Catholic school, all under the Indian Department, and one public school, and the children are taken every year from there to the Industrial schools at Elkhorn, Kenora, Brandon, &c. There are six churches and chapels; one of the churches will seat over 400 people. At the last confirmation service of the English church two years ago, held there by Bishop Matheson, over sixty were confirmed. As far as the Indians are concerned they are just as well educated as any in the northwest provinces or the Dominion.

Now, I propose to say a word as to the charge made by the hon. gentleman that 90 per cent of the receipts for the 338 patents which were issued were forgeries. This is a very series charge and, for my part, I do not care to accept it until it is proved. I do not care to accept it because it is such an easy thing to prove. I think the point was well taken by the Minister of the Interior that it was a criminal offence, and as such it should be dealt with by the Justice Department in Manitoba. That being so, and it also being true that any political caper on the part of the Liberal party would lead them into trouble-the Attorney General of Manitoba could be counted on to look after these gentlemen, particularly if they were Liberals. That has been

my experience, that has been the experience of every Liberal in Manitoba that he could bother in the least degree no matter whether there was a case or not. The hon. member for Selkirk has made a serious charge, he knows the remedy, he knows where his friends are, the machinery is there, the money is there, (public opinion is there, and public opinion will be behind him and will be behind the Attorney General, no matter whether we agree with him politically ox not, if he takes the proper course, which I think it is his duty to take and put where they belong the man or men who were parties to such a thing as that the rights of the Indians should be taken from them through forged deals. If this statement that 90 per cent of 338 patents were forged be true, it is sufficiently serious to call for action on the part of the law department of the government of Manitoba.

As far as the affidavits are concerned, I notice that they are * all those of Indians and not of white men. I mention this only for the reason that the hon. member would have us understand that this was away from politics, that it was a matter only of the poor, down-trodden, suffei-ing Indian and particularly of the Indian in his county. If it were as independent of politics as he would have us believe, my information is that he spent all of the Christmas holidays getting these affidavits, which he had a right to do and I do not object to it, with the commissioner, who was just as good a Tory as he was, land who acted as the hon. gentleman's agent in the last general election. I think [DOT]that it is apparent that it is a party move *on the part of the hon. gentleman. If he ban make any move whereby he can 'strengthen himself in the eyes of his constituents that would only be fair and, as 'far as that is concerned, I would do anything that would strengthen myself in the eyes of my constituents; but I believe he is on the wrong track, and I believe that the Indians of,St. Peter's reserve 'were fairly and honestly dealt with at that time in the interest of the settlers, in the interests of the townspeople, and in the interests of the Indians themselves, in taking them away from influences which were detrimental to their welfare and prosperity and placing them in a better position to make a living than where they were adjacent to the town of Selkirk. And above all, that the price of the land was just as good and, as has been proven, better than was paid the following June for school land just alongside of it and in some cases with only the road allowance between.

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,Mr. Speaker, last night from my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) we listened, at some length, to what in my judgment was one of the most forcible, most convincing and most damaging arraignment of the government which it has yet been my privilege to hear in this House; and to-day the government has substantially pleaded guilty to the indictment. As spokesman for the government, the hon. Minister of the Interior .(Mr. Oliver) addressed this House at some length to-day, but his remarks were so feeble that the broadest charity would fail to dignify them into an argument. His efforts were so feeble indeed as to be positively pitiable to all his friends in this House. The case goes substantially undefended. All the principal facts brought out by my hon. friend from Selkirk have gone unanswered. It is true, the Minister of the Interior took up some time in dealing with matters which were comparatively immaterial. It is true, my hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. Molloy) made some remarks just before dinner which, owing to the defective accoustics of this House and the distance between him and me, I was unable to catch distinctly. He may have brought forward some arguments which I was unable to hear. But I was close enough to the Minister of the Interior to hear all that he said, and I repeat that the material facts charged against the government last night by my hon. friend from Selkirk have remained unanswered; and, with your permission and kindness, Mr. Speaker, I will endeavour to substantiate that before I sit down. What were the conditions which 'confronted the government of this country in the fall of 1907, respecting the St. Peter's band of Indians? In the year 1871, under treaty, a number of Crees, Chippewas and Saultaux were gathered together on this reserve, situated on the Red river about 25 miles below the city of Winnipeg, a strip of land 4 miles wide on either side of the river, and extending 10 or 12 miles in length. In the fall of 1907, about 1,300 Indians were living on that reserve. They, or their ancestors, had lived on it as a separate location since the year 1871. The whole reserve contains about 55,000 acres-, of which about 5,000 acres were patented to whites either prior or subsequent to 1871. A trolley line runs between Winnipeg and Selkirk, and a steam railway Tuns on either side of the river. Selkirk is a thriving town of about 3,000 inhabitants. This reserve extends right up to the boundary of the town of Selkirk. Selkirk was at the head of navigation on the Red river, but now, owing to artificial

structures, navigation has been extended to the city of Winnipeg. So that we have here about 50,000 acres of land situated within 25 miles of a city which in a very few years will contain half a million of inhabitants, and is destined to be the metropolis of Canada. All the 50,000 acres is as good land as the sun shines on. 1 venture to think that if the hon. Minister of the Interior owned that strip in his individual right, looking forward to the possibilities of its value in the near future, he would not sell an acre of it for less than $50. Let me read a few words of some of the Indian agents of this government and of former governments. I want to read first a few lines from the l'atei Ebenezer MeColl. He was a Liberal of the old school, a resident of the constituency which I have the honour to represent. He was appointed by the Liberal administration in power here prior to 1878. During the 18 years of the late Conservative regime he enioyed the fullest confidence of Sir John A. Macdonald and those who succeeded him in the premiership of Canada-a man whose honour and integrity could not be questioned by any one who knew him. I want to read a few words from his report, written at Winnipeg, on July 31, 1900. He was at that time, and had been for many years, inspector of Indian agencies. I want-to read this especially in answer to a remark of the hon. Minister of the Interior to the effect that these Indians were degenerating. Mr. MeColl said among other things:

There seems to be a growing tendency amongst the Indians to attend divine service. Their interest in sncli matters was quite evident to me at St. Peter's during the time we_ were there paying the annuities, when religions _ services were held every evening in 1he adjoining chanel. These services, I noticed, were all well attended and were attentively and hespectfullyl listened to. It is almost a quarter of a century since I first visited these reserves, and in that time I have seen some marked changes. Twenty-five years ago St. Peter's was nothing hut a string of huts and tepees scattered along the hanks of the Red river. The people were living upon fish, and spent their time hunting and trapping small game. There most pretentious vehicle was the Red River cart, whose creaking could be heard for miles crossing the silent prairie. To-day there are very few, if any, thatched-roofed houses. The buildings are shingled, well fenced, surrounded by gardens, with stables and storehouses adjoining.

Twenty-five years ago the small houses had but one room in which all lived and slept regardless of relationship. Now the houses are divided into compartments. There has been an almost incredible advance made along the line of moral reform.
I would like my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior to take the trouble to read some of the reports sent him from the agents and inspectors of these Indian agencies.

Then we have some remarks from Mr. John Semmons, Indian agent. He says:

All three of these places-St. Peter's reserve is one-are situated in areas of excel- * lent land, suitable for farming and stockraising purposes, while at the same time they are adjacent to water, so that the natives may enjoy all the advantages of sailing and fishing. All the conditions are there to contribute to the welfare and happiness of the people.
That was in the year 1903.
We have tried to teach them to observe the regulations of the department which have reference to the preservation of health, and for the most part have had their co-operation.

Some of the best soil in Manitoba is to be found in St. Peter's. All this is protected by a fringe of wood to the west and northwest. The three larger bodies have beautiful churches, resident clergymen, and organized work. The Indian, as I find him, is a religious person and well disposed towards that which is good.
I have another report from the inspector of the Indian agencies, dated 28th December, 1903, in which, speaking of St. Peter's reserve, he says:

It is all first-class land. The area is about 48,000 acres or nearly two townships, and is oil first-class land, rich black soil of great depth. It is a mixed open and bush country with some very fine hay land on the north part of the reserve.

So that I hope we shall not hear any more about large portions of this reserve being worthless, when we have this inspector saying it is all first-class land, rich, black soil of great depth. The last report we have was in 1907 from a gentleman called Lewis. In that report, which is very lengthy, he says:

The land is a loam with a clay subsoil. During the winter of 1906 the market of Selkirk was almost entirely supplied with hay brought in by the St. Peter's Indians, from which they derive a large revenue. During the winter of 1906, permission was given by the department to cut and sell dry wood. 3,500 cords were cut and marketed. There are five day schools in this reserve. Out of a population of about 1,300, there are not many drunkards, and the band may be said to be temperate.

I listened to the remarks of the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) this afternoon with a great deal of interest, and I am sure that every one who heard him must have reached the conclusion that he has not the faintest conception of the duties of a guardian towards his ward. It has been defined on good authority what
those duties are, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall quote from that authority:

The duties of a guardian towards his ward are generally to exercise the same prudence and foresight which a good business man would use in the management of his o\*n fortune, though under more guarded restraint.

Let us look a little further to ascertain what parliament and the people of this country have defined the duties of the guardians of these wards to be. Parliament has declared that the government of Canada shall be the guardians of the Indians of this country, and I want to say here that I have been unable to find any authority whatever for this or any other government in Canada making a present of public lands to the unenfranchised Indians. I do not believe that authority exists, in any law or statute in this country, for the government making a grant in fee I simple to the non-enfranchised Ilfidian. Let us look at a few sections of the Indian Act and see what we can gather from them. Every line of this statute, composed! of 195 sections, declares that the government of Canada shall be the guardians of these Indians and that these Indians shall be the wards of the government. Every line of this statute declares that it is the duty of the government to look after these wards as a guardian would look after the interests of the infant left to his care These Indians are but infants. The hon. gentleman a few weeks ago spoke of them as understanding business transactions just as well as the average member of this House, and he spoke as if he expected some one to believe him. But the facts set forth last night by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and not denied, have satisfied every one in this House that the Indians on that reserve had not reached that state of intelligence to enable them to look after themselves. We have in the fourth section of the Indian Act these words:

The Minister of the Interior or the head of any other department appointed for that purpose by the Governor in Council shall be the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, and shall as such have control and management of all the lands and property of tile Indians in Canada.

So that the people of Canada have placed in the hands of the government the management and control of all the lands and property of the Indians in Canada, and the Minister of the Interior, as Superintendent General of the Indian Affairs, is the man under whose control the lands and properties of all the Indians in Canada are. And the Minister of the Interior, as Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, is the man who is primarily liable to the people of
Canada to-day, and the government, through him, is responsible for what I regard as one of the most contemptible schemes and swindles that the people of this country ever witnessed.

The Indian Act does give the power to make patents to Indians in certain instances, but let me show what is required of an Indian before he can become entitled to a patent in fee simple of any land in this country, and you will see from this statute how carefully the interests of the Indian have been protected by the parliament of Canada.

Seo. 108. Whenever any male Indian or unmarried Indian woman, of the full age of 21 years, makes application to the Superintendent General to be enfranchised, the Superintendent General should instruct the agent of the band of which the applicant is a member, to call upon the latter to furnish a certificate, under oath, before a judge of any court of justice, by the priest, clergyman or minister of the religious denomination to which the applicant belongs, or by a stipendiary magistrate, or two justices of the peace, to the effect that to the best of the knowledge and belief of the deponent or deponents, the applicant for enfranchisement is, and has been for at least five years previously, a person of good moral character, temperate in his or her habits, and of sufficient intelligence to be qualified to hold land in fee simple, and otherwise to exercise all the rights and privileges of an enfranchised person.

That first section requires an affidavit sworn before a judge by a priest, clergyman or minister that the applicant for enfranchisement has for five years been a person of good moral character, that he has for five years been temperate in his habits, and that he has sufficient intelligence to be qualified to hold land in fee simple and otherwise to exercise all the rights and privileges of an enfranchised person. Without any of these safeguards, the government, on the representation of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, deeded 21,000 acres of land to these Indians without any inquiry from priest or minister or any one else as to whether they were men of good moral character, who had been temperate for five years and had sufficient intelligence to entitle them to obtain their deed in fee simple. Other sections are:

column2: Upon receipt of such certificate, the agent shall, with the least possible delay, submit the same to a council of the band of which the applicant is a member, and he should then inform the Indians assembled at such council, that thirty days will be given within which affidavits made before a judge or a stipendiary magistrate will be received, containing reasons if there are any of a personal character affecting the applicant, why such enfranchisement should not be granted to the applicant.

Such letters patent shall contain a provision that such Indian shall not have power to sell, lease or otherwise alienate the land except with the sanction of the Governor in Counoil.
In such case9, compliance with provisions of this part respecting leases or surrender of lands in a reserve shall not be neoessary.

Every such Indian shall, before the issue of such letters patent, declare to the Superintendent General the name and surname by which he wishes to be enfranchised and thereafter known, and on his receiving such letters patent in such name and surname, he shall be held to be enfranchised, and he shall thereafter be known as such name or surname; and, if such Indian is a married man, his wife and minor unmarried children shall also be held to be enfranchised.

From the date of such letters patent the provisions of this part and of any Act or law making any distinction between the legal rights, privileges, disabilities and liabilities of Indians and those of His Majesty's other subjects, shall cease to apply to such Indian, or hi9 wife, or his minor unmarried children, and he and they shall no longer be deemed Indians within the meaning of the laws relating to Indians, except in so far as regards their right to participate in the annuities and interest moneys, and rents and councils of the band to which they belong.

Whenever any member of a band, for three years immediately succeeding the date on which he was granted letters patent from his enfranchisement as aforesaid, or for any longer period that the Superintendent General deems necessary, by his exemplary good conduct and management of property proves that he is qualified to receive his share of the moneys of such band, the Governor in Council may on the report of the Superintendent General to that effect, order that the said Indian be paid his share of the capital funds at the credit of the band, or his share of the principal of the annuities of the band, estimated as yielding five per cent of such moneys as are provided for the purpose by parliament.

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,So that the people have declared that before an Indian, shall be entitled to receive a title in fee simple to a piece of land, the priest or clergyman and the agent shall make affidavits that they have known the man for five years to be a man of good moral character, of temperate habits and of sufficient intelligence to be entrusted with the management of real estate. Then the band has to be called together and notified that application has been made and the band are given thirty days to show why the applicant should not get a patent, to show that he is not an Indian of good moral character, that he is of intemperate habits, that he is not an Indian of sufficient intelligence to be entrusted with the handling of realty. Then the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs may locate him on a lot as a probationer for three years longer before he is entitled to his patent. Thus he must have been a man of good moral character for eight years, a man of temperate habits for eight years, a man who has displayed intelligence in his private affairs for eight years, before he will become entitled to a patent, and in addition to that he must add on three years more before he is entitled to receive as an individual freeman his share of the money in the Indian fund. The people of this country, guardians of the Indians, who are mere children, have surrounded these children, children of nature, by these safeguards. How in the world did the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, the government of this country, surround these men with safeguards when they gave patents to lands amounting to 21,000 acres, knowing full well, as Mr. Frank Pedley, the Deputy Minister, wrote to his chief, that they would, in a very short time, alienate all these lands?

Are we fair in drawing the inference that when this government undertook to secure a surrender of that reserve which had belonged to these Indians, and to deed to them 21,000 acres of land, no evidence of their moral character, no evidence of their temperate habits, no evidence of their intelligence to handle their own affairs, no probation for three years as required by the parliament of Canada-are we right, I say, in inferring that when these 21,000 acres of land were, by the government of this country deeded over to these children of nature, the government knew and understood that in a very short time they would become an easy prey to the unscrupulous whites, more advanced in intelligence, while less amenable to conscience? Is it a fair inference, yea, is it not rather expressly proved by the deputy minister when he writes to the Minister of the Interior saying, I anticipate that in a very short time these Indians will alienate their land to the whites? So I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this government, when they determined to con-

vey 21,000 acres of land to men of whom they knew nothing as to their moral character, as to their temperate habits, as to their thrift, as to their intelligence, the government became a party to the dissipation of 21,000 acres of the public domain of this country? The Minister of the Interior tries to shelter himself behind Chief Justice Howell, of Manitoba. Well, I am not very much concerned about Chief Justice Howell, I have not had the advantage, or disadvantage of an acquaintance with him. But I have lived long enough to know that a chief justiceship bestowed by this administration carries no guarantee against partisanship, or for wisdom, humanity, or common, every day honesty. So we do not propose to deal with the Chief Justice of Manitoba, 'we propose to deal with the government of this country who is responsible for what has been done in this regard. Let me read to you a few more sections to show in some more detail the way in which the government looks after these Indians, or are supposed to look after them, because in this case they did not look after them at all. Those Indians were by this government treated with a callous indifference and cruelty that excites the sympathy and indignation of every man capable of distinguishing Tight from wrong. I will read section 38:

column2: The Governor in Council may make regulations for prohibiting the sale, barter, exchange or gift by any band or irregular band of Indians, or by any Indian of any band or irregular band, in the province of Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta, or the Territories, of any grain or root crops, or other produce grown upon any reserve, and may further provide that such sale, barter, exchange or gift shall be null and void, unless the same are made in accordance with such regulations.

No person shall buy or otherwise acquire from any band or irregular band of Indians, or from any Indian, any grain, root crops, or other produce from upon any reserve in the province of Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta, or the Territories.

If any such grain or root crops, or other produce as aforesaid, are unlawfully in the possession of any person within the intent and meaning of this part, or of any regulations made by the Governor m Council under this part, any person acting under the authority, either general or special, of the Superintendent General, may, with such assistance in that behalf as he thinks necessary, seize and take possession of the same; and he shall deal therewith as the Superintendent General, or any officer or person thereunto by him authorized, directs.
The Governor in Council may make regulations for prohibiting the cutting, carrying away or removing from any reserve or special reserve, of any hard or sugar maple tree or sapling.

column1: 43. No person shall barter directly or indirectly with any Indian on a reseive in the j rovince of Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta, or in the Territories, or sell to any
such Indian any goods or supplies, cattle or ether animals without the special license in writing of the Superintendent General.

column2: The Superintendent General may, at any time, revoke the license by him given.

Upon prosecution of any ofiender against the provisions of this and last preceding section, the evidence of the Indian to whom the sale was made, and the production to, or view by, the magistrate or Indian agent of the article or animal sold, shall be sufficient evidence on which to convict.

column1: So, Mr. Speaker, I think I have read enough from this Act to show that the parliament of this country has declared in every section of it, indeed in every line of it, that in the opinion of this country the unenfrachised Indians are not capable of protecting themselves against the schemes and tricks of the unscrupulous whites; and I charge here that the government of this country have grossly neglected their duty with reference to the St. Peter's band of Indians. Now, in 1907 it seems that some one desired that this reserve should be surrendered. The evidence, so far as we have heard it, goes to show that only one man requested that the Indians should be asked to surrender their reserve, and that was the man who represented that constituency in this House as a supporter of the present government. He had been an Indian agent for some years, he resigned, became a candidate, was elected, and sat in this House and supported our friends on the other side; and when he was subsequently defeated they returned him to his office as Indian agent. He is the man who made some of these reports I have read to you. I have not been able to find any authority in this statute, or anywhere else-there may be some, but I have not been able to find any authority for this or any government of Canada to deed in fee simple to an unenfranchised Indian any part of this country. Here the government deeded 21,000 acres of land to these men, knowing, expressly anticipating that they would become the easy prey of land speculators, and that they would speedily dissipate the small pittance that they would get from this land. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to every man in this House, whether he sits on this side, or on the other side of it, can he, in his judgment, and in his conscience say that the government was right in deeding 21,000 acres of land to these children of nature who knew not how to take care of it, and who, they anticipated, would immediately sell and dissipate it?

The motion before the House to-day is that the members of this House should express condemnation of the conduct of the government in that regard. Two questions arise, as I understand it. The first one is the policy of the government in desiring to get a surrender from these Indians

and to send them back 150 or 200 miles into the wilderness again. That is one question. There may be some argument in favour of it. There have been five schools and many churches maintained on* that reserve for years. Many of us are asked to contribute. To do what? To guide, if possible, these children of nature to a higher intelligence, to self-control, to good citizenship and the evidence of -Ebenezer McColl is that these Indians had made satisfactory progress, slow, of course, as the progress in such matters always must be, but that they were making progress in intelligence, in the line of moral reform and temperance. Then, the first question is as to what we think of the policy of gathering up these men and women who have been living there for generations and driving them and their children from the rude but happy homes of their childhood away back into the wilderness-no friends, no home, no house, no wigwam! Does that strike us as treating these people as we profess to treat them as Christian people, striving to lead them higher in intelligence, higher in morality, striving to lead them to a higher life of self-control and good citizenship. Is that the way to do it? After you have kept on for fifty or sixty years, teaching them in schools and churches, educating them, bringing them along gradually you send them away 200 miles into the wilderness. Begin all over again, build more schools and churches and send more missionaries there! That is one view of it. But, that is not the more serious question. The more serious question is the manner in which this surrender was secured. The Minister of Interior to-day dwelt largely on the word ' bribery '-not so strong on that point as he was five months ago, but still he showed considerable strength in his objection to the idea of these men being bribed. What was it if it was not bribery? You sometimes give a child five cents if it will take some disagreeable medicine. Bribery ! You give it a candy and cause it to do something. Bribery! What is bribery? Something given to pervert the judgment and get an individual to do that which he otherwise would not do. That is what bribery is and I say that every one who had anything to do with this transaction that is presented here to-night and not denied by any one from the Minister of the Interior and Chief Justice Howell, all the way down, was guilty of bribery in inducing these Indians to give up their homes. We had it stated here last night in several affidavits how they were induced to surrender their reserve. It was stated in affidavits here last) night that they were given but one day's notice. That has not been denied. The Minister of the Interior said something this afternoon-

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,It would be interesting to know on what ground the Minister of the Interior makes the denial. I would very much prefer to have the denial of some one who was there and knows the facts. It was stated here upon an affidavit that there was but one day's notice given, which was Sunday, and that the meeting was held on Monday in a room so small that only a small portion of the Indians who gathered together could get in. It was stated on affidavit that the Deputy Minister told the Indians that he had $5,000 in his satchel, and that if they vrould consent to the surrender they would get that $5,000, and that if they would not consent to it he would gather up his grip and go back to Ottawa, Where did the money come from? It was your money and mine they took away to buy up these poor children of the forest, to surrender their homes, the homes of their wives and their little ones, the rude huts in which their children were born and in which their children had grown up. Still, he says that we must not call that bribery. If I could find a word of ten times the strength of bribery, I would use it on this occasion and use it with the greatest justification. It was stated here last night in a sworn statement that a gentleman went out of the little school house and, in the Cree language, said to the Indians: Those who want $90, go over with the chief and councillors, and those who do not want $90 go over on the other side. Now, Mr. Speaker, that was stated here last night under oath, but that was not the first time it was stated. It was stated in this House, in the presence of the Minister of the Interior, nearly five months ago. If that statement were not true, the Minister of the Interior would have some affidavits here to deny it. Chief Justice Howell was there on that occasion more than two years ago. The minister knew this charge of bribery was made, this charge about the $90, this charge that only a few Indians knew what was going on in this little building, because being outside they did not hear anything, because five months ago it had been brought to his attention in this House by Mr. Bradbury. If it were not true, how is it that we have not an affidavit from Chief Justice Howell denying it? The minister stated this afternoon that he had not heard anything about some of these things until he heard it last night. Well, suppose he had not, tne Deputy Minister, Frank Pedley, is in the city to-day. How is it that he has not an affidavit from him to the effect that what was stated here last night is not correct, because Mr. Pedley is the man who was stated to have told the Indians that: I have a grip here with

$5,000 in it; if you vote for the surrender you will get $5,000; if you do not I will go back to Ottawa, take it with me, and you will not get a cent. Bribery! He is indignant because we say they bribed these poor Indians who sacrificed their homes, friends, teachers, priests, everything that they had been taught to prize most highly in life. Bribery! Then they gave them the deed of 80 acres of land that they knew they were going to sell. The Minister of the Interior has the courage to sit in his seat now and laugh at the idea that these poor Indians were bribed. Could he go further than that? My friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) dissected the 49th section, which he thought required a majority of all the male Indians of a band at a meeting assembled, of the full age of 21 years, to surrender.

Now, Sir, I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) that that 'is the meaning of that section, although I _ do not say that it is so beyond all question. But there have been decisions in our courts on statutes worded in substance as this statute is worded, holding that the majority of the whole people are required to express their opinion under such conditions, and not merely a majority of those present at a meeting. I believe that to be the meaning of this section. I believe it is to be fair according to the spirit of the law even if it be not according to the letter of the law. Who, for one moment, with a particle of humanity in his soul would get a few Indians together and by offering them $90 a piece, and 16 acres of land a piece, would induce them to sign away the rights of their neighbours, their wives, and their children? It makes the blood in one's veins boil with indignaton when we think of the manner in which these simple people were cheated, and yet the government professes to be indignant because we say they bribed them. This land was deeded to the Indians, and you have heard the evidence. It was sold here and there and elsewhere, a few acres at a time, just as we would expect a child or an Indian to do it. If the Indian wanted $5 or $10 he would sign anything to gratify his present requirements. If !he had a good big dinner he would lie down and sleep for a few days never thinking of how he would get a dinner for the morrow. We all know that is the nature of the Indian. No one knew that better than the Minister of the Interior, no one knew that better than Chief Justice Howell; no one knew better than these two gentlemen when they gave these children of nature a deed of land _ that they would dissipate it within a few ' days. The Indians parted with the lands at $5 an acre taken out in truck-land situated as it is, all the very .best of land, land which I venture to say neither the 227

Minister of the Interior nor the hon. member from Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) would have sold for less than $50 an acre if they had a patent for it. That is the land that was dissipated at $5 an acre by the Indian. The Indian has squandered the money and the Indian is on our hands now. Well, Sir, it simply meant taking 21,000 acres of the peoples' land and giving it to a few land sharks. That is the substance of the whole matter. What more did we have? We had this sale. The Minister of the Interior was asked two or three times why the advertisement was not continued in the newspapers up to the date of the sale, and we heard no answer. I have said that it is the duty of a guardian in the management of an estate to exercise the same prudence and foresight that he would use in managing his own fortune. I want to ask you, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. gentlemen of this House, if, the Minister of the Interior had been the owner in his own individual right of these 48,000 acres, he would have advertised them for sale and sold them for whatever was offered? No, he is one of the last men in this House to do a thing of that kind. What do we do when we have a piece of land to sell under mortgage, or for an infant?. We offer it for sale at public auction in the older parts of the country, we get at least three men who have no personal interest to serve to value that land and make an affidavit as to its value, and when we tell the auctioneer that unless the bid reaches a certain price he is not to declare the land sold. Is not that what the Minister of the Interior would have done if this land had been his own? Is there a man [DOT]in this House who believes he would not have done that very thing were it his own case? And Sir, if he would do it in his .own case, he has been guilty of a breach of trust for not doing it in this case. We have an official in the province of Ontario who is called the official guardian, and whose duty it is to look after the interests of infants. That official never allows the land of an infant to be sold unless he has affidavits as to its value from three independent men whom he knows to be reliable and who have no personal interest in the matter. Then there is a reserve bid fixed. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, I ask the hon. members of this House if the government of this country in this transaction have discharged their plain duty. as guardians of the Indian wards of the country? Is there a man in this House who can say they have? Is there a man in this House who would not vote condemnation of this transaction if he were to follow the dictates of his judgment, and his conscience? I don't think there , is a single one.

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,I want to treat the hon. member fairly; I hope I have not misinterpreted him. At any rate, I think I may say for myself, if the hon. gentleman repudiates it, that it is the most serious charge which has been brought against this government since this parliament was elected. It is the first opportunity that the opposition has had of attacking the Minister of the Interior in regard to the administration of his department. The very bitterness which they have shown in their speeches and their vehemence of utterance show that they do not expect to have another chance for a very long time. Let me direct the attention of the House, as my hon. friend has done, to the original conditions under which this reserve of St. Peter's was laid out. In the year 1871 a treaty was made with the Chippewa and Cree tribes, of Indians for setting aside the reserve which is now known -as the St. Peter's reserve. In that treaty there was this term:

If at tlie date of the execution of this treaty there are any settlers within, the hounds of any of the lands reserved, Her Majesty reserves the right to deal with such settlers as she deems just so as not to diminish the extent of land allotted to the Indians.

I think that clause in the original treaty explains to a great degree the reasons for the surrender which we are discussing tonight. It is a matter of record that from time to time claims were made by those who had already settled in this tract set aside for the reserve prior to the makine-of the treaty. Some of them were halfbreeds, some of them were Indians, and I suppose some of them were whites. At any rate when this whole tract of land was set aside, there were claims admitted by the government between 1871 and 1906, when the Hon. Chief Justice Howell was appointed commissioner, which amounted to some 5,400 acres. As I understand it, these small parcels of land scattered throughout the reserve and occupied by enfranchised Indians and whites, were a menace to the administration of the reserve by the Indian Department. In this clause I have just read you will see that the Crown was to deal with such settlers as had obtained rights within this area in such manner as the Crown might think just, so as not to diminish the extent of 227J .

land allowed to the Indians. There were many claims placed before the government by those who had their rights before they became members of the band which subsequently settled upon these lands, and Mr. Chief Justice Howell was appointed commissioner. The very fact that claims to the extent of 5,400 acres had already been dealt with shows that they were considerable and that Chief Justice Howell had evidently a very considerable Work cut out for him. His investigation resulted in the agreement to surrender, which has been read by the Minister of the Interior. The reasons for obtaining such surrender are easily seen. It was to extinguish these claims which were before the government and which were held by members of the band who were on this land. There was also the general reason, which no doubt has always prevailed, for the removal of any Indian band when civilization encroaches upon them, and when it is better for themselves that they should be removed, and a great deal better for the settlers who live near the reserves that these reserves should be thrown open for settlement and the land cultivated, as white people know how to .cultivate.

I want to point out that this 48,000 acres includes not only lands which were set apart as a reserve for the Indian band, but also whatever lands were in dispute between the Indians or half breeds and the government, and which claims arose prior to the setting aside of this tract in 1871, under the treaty I have just referred to. I would also point out that the agreement specially provides that there shall be no diminishing of land allowed to the Indians by virtue of any land being granted out of the reserve to those who have proper claims. In the subsequent settlement, in which the Indians obtained a reserve of 75,000 acres towards Lake Winnipeg, they got this additional land so that if their reserve should be diminished by reason of the admission of any further claims, this new reserve would compensate them for this diminution.

There are three points upon which the opposition criticise the agreement of surrender obtained from the Indians during the negotiations of Chief Justice Howell. They criticise the grant in severalty. I would point out that if any of these people who liye upon this reserve were entitled to any rights whatever in severalty, they were entitled to them before they became members of the band under the treaty of 1871, and consequently they were entitled to them in severalty; and if they were entitled to them in severalty, then, I think, it is a fair conclusion that, being the same people, they were entitled to them in severalty at the time this new arrangement was made.
There is also this objection taken to the

terms of the surrender, and that is that the sale of the land granted in severalty should have been conducted under government supervision. So far as I am aware this was not one of the terms in the agreement made at the instance of Chief Justice Howell. I understand it was in the original agreement; and having been in the original agreement was submitted to the Indians, who refused to accede to it and insisted that they should be seized of the lands in severalty without any interference whatever on the part of the government. For the reasons I have pointed out, it does seem to me that the government was justified in adjusting claims which should have been made prior to 1871 in severalty and in settling these claims in severalty in 1907.
The third objection made to this agreement is the provision for an advance of $5j000 on account of half of the proceeds. Let me read this extract from the agreement :
The department shall advance, at the time of the surrender, the sum of $5,000 to be repaid out of the first money received from the sale of the land.

This evidently is the $5,000 which Mr. Pedley had in his grip and which was referred to by my hon. friend in very vehement terms as bribery. That is a very strong term to use. .It is one which should not be used except under the greatest provocation, and I wish to point out that, under the Indian Act, the government is authorized to pay over to the Indians a sum not exceeding 50 per cent of the proceeds of any lands sold. So my hon. friends opposite use the term bribery with reference to a matter which is authorized by Act of parliament.

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,I regret exceedingly that I was not able to closely follow the argument, if you may call it such, of the hon. member for Saskatoon. However, there was a significance to his last remark which at least deserves reply. Apparently by that remark he wished to enunicate a new doctrine that a government are in no case bound to investigate any charge unless first of all they believe that charge is true, because he says that unless he believed the charge made and substantiated by evidence by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), he would not recommend it to be investigated; and in that of course he only follows the cue of the Minister of the Interior himself, who enunciated that doctrine. If we are to follow any such theory as that we might just as well start out by enunciating that there are to be no more investigations under this government, because no government I ever heard of would first of all announce that they believed the charges against themselves. But that statement of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Mc-Craney) was not one whit more absurb than has been the whole theory of the government in their defence against these charges. As my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) said, the only skill that has characterized the members who have spoke on behalf of the Minister of

the Interior, and the minister himself, has been in evading the charges levelled against his department. His department is charged with resorting to improper means in procuring this surrender. They stand charged with having procured that surrender by dangling dollars before the Indian chiefs and before the Indians themselves, and by improperly putting a vote to the Indian band. If it is proper to dangle $5,000 before the eyes of the Indians in order to induce them to vote away their heritage, then there can be no charge on that score against this government. If it is proper to 'put a vote as to the surrender of a band by offering $90 to all who voted for it, then on that score also there is no charge against the government, and there is nothing to investigate. It is proven and admitted that the man who put the vote indicated to the band that those who voted for it would get the $90.

Now there are two things that emerge clear from this discussion. The first is that a band of Indians were in possession of 48,000 acres of land in St. Peter's reserve, and that the government desired to move them further north, and did so at a cost to this country of 95,000 acres of land, and many, many ""thousands of dollars. The second is that a band of speculators is now safely sheltered on the other side of the ledger and rich for life. Now those are two premises that must go undisputed; if any *one wishes to dispute them, let him stand up. Now the government say. That may be the case, the speculators may be rich and the country may be out, but we are not responsible. And why? First of all, they put the august personage of the Chief Justice of Manitoba between them and harm. The Minister of the Interior, when this charge was first levelled at him last fall, struggled for a considerable time to assert that the man responsible was the Chief Justice of Manitoba, and that if we dared say a word about this transaction, we were impugning the honesty of the chief justice. We are not concerned with the Chief Justice of Manitoba, we are concerned with the parties who carried out the transaction and who are responsible to us and to the people of this country. 'Now to procure the surrender of that reserve it was necessary, first -of all, to use the means I have outlined, it was necessary to send a responsible officer of this govem-fment, the man who sits next to the minister himself, out there with a bag of $5,000 to bribe them by the looks of the green.

304443,ca.proc.d.1910-04-14.14.2.227,1910-04-14,d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2,ca.m.4870,Mr. MEIGHEN.,,SUPPLY-ST. PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,I am not at all shirking responsibility. The attitude of the minister shows that he is uneasy under this charge, and I think that does credit to his honour. Now, I said the result was that the country was out the land, the country was out the money, and that the speculators were rich for life. But where is the Indian? The Indian was left to be the prey of the speculators. By what authority have the government abandoned him? By what authority did the government flee from its position as their guardian for a matter of commercial advantage? Does the Minister of the Interior claim that he is justified in abdicating his position as guardian of the Indians of this country? Is he their guardian when he places in the hands of an Indian 16, or 100, or 180 acres of land, as he has done. Is he their guardian when he allows them to dispose of that land, contrary to law, to a band of greedy speculators? Where does the minister get his authority for abandoning the trust, for fleeing away from his duty as he did in this case? The Minister of the Interior has not answered that, nor has the member for Saskatoon, who is a lawyer; neither of them have answered the charge made to-night that they illegally granted those lands to the Indians. Is there any authority in the Indian Act for granting land to an unenfranchised Indian? The Indian Act is the statute of this country, framed in order to fortify these helpless people against speculators and greedy whites. By what author-Mr. MEIGHEN

ity does the Minister of the Interior throw down these fortifications and leave him a victim to the invader? Why does not the member for Saskatoon, instead of quoting what some adjoining lands formerly sold for, answer the real charge against the government? If there is one duty, if there is one office more sacred to the government of any country than another, it is the office and the duty of guarding the tew as it is written. The government's first duty is to administer the law and to see that it is obeyed. How do they expect the people to hold sacred the law or to obey it if they themselves are the first to violate it? Of what value is it that this parliament, as the representative of the people, should construct a fortification guarding these helpless people from speculators, if the minister can throw it down at his will, or at the behest of his friends the speculators? Why are we sitting here to-night to legislate if he, at his will, can violate our legislation? I cannot see any authority, I cannot conceive that there could be any legal authority, for the grant that was made.

The law of the country in the Indian Act is the only reference to Indians as far as I know, and that law distinctly says that the Indian cannot be granted land. The Indian is described as a person who is not only incompetent to hold land, but he is incompetent to buy chattels. Section after section of the Act forbids individuals to buy chattels from Indians, and to sell them chattels except under the supervision of the minister. A man is not allowed to go to an Indian, and sell him two chickens: unless he has authority by license from the Governor in Council. By what authority then does the minister not only permit men to sell them oxen, and hay and everything that they imagine an Indian wants, but also to go to them and dicker with them, drunk or sober, for their land? Surely no justification has been made out. No justification can be made out. There can be no exigencies, there can be no difficulty, there can be no commercial advantage sufficiently pressing to warrant the minister in violating this law. I would like, before this debate ends, that that point should be answered. I would like to see the authority under any statute of this country for granting lands to unenfranchised Indians. If there is such authority the Indian Act is a nullity. What was the result of all this? What was the result of leaving these Indians the prey of speculators? There was a man by the name of Tracy, who got hundreds and thousands of acres of these lands and he paid on the average of $5.55 an acre. I have figured up most of the return brought down by the minister, and indeed it is not complete, as to these sales, and the figures show that the average was $5.55 an acre. And how did Tracy pay them? He paid them by selling them their own hay, he

paid them by selling them cattle at fabulous prices, and everything else on an equal scale, contrary to the provisions of the Indian Act, and the minister has absolutely refused to interfere, and protect them or prosecute Tracy for his violation of the Act. The minister, first of all, asked the Indian agent or inspector, Mr. Swin-ford, to look into this matter, and what did Swinford do*1 I do not know what his instructions, at least- his verbal instructions, were, but I want to point out one thing. Mr. Swinford reported that all this charge about Tracy palming off goods on the Indians instead of paying them their money, was false. He says in his report, and let the Minister of the Interior note this, that over 80 per cent of the moneys that Tracy agreed to pay were paid in cash, or orders on stores. I thought that was rather strange looking at Tracy's accounts which are fearfully and wonderfully made. I figured them up, and they certainly show no such result as that which Mr. Swinford states. They show that instead of Tracy paying them 80 per cent in money and orders on stores he paid them less than 30' per cent. He paid them 72 per cent of their money in hay, and such like. Only 28 per cent of that $5 per acre ever reached the Indian at all in the form of cash or orders. That is the accuracy with which Mr. Swinford reported. That is a remarkable thing, but what more do we find? What was the condition of the Indian under this treaty? I find one case of Mr. Tracy's dealings which I can give the minister. There was a poor fellow who had sold Tracy land for which he was to receive $420. Tracy sold him his own hay, etc., until he made up $260 of the $420. Then he gave him $46 in cash, and orders on stores. The Indian proceeded to get drunk on the $46, and then Tracy paid $58.40, and $96, and all for plate glass windows and police court fines on account of the drunk that the Indian got out of the $46. That is only a sample. Moneys that these Indians have been paid have been paid by Tracy, and other speculators in the police court fines for plate glass windows, and other damage that these men have caused while under the influence of liquor. Could anything within the conception of the minister justify the leaving of these Indians to treatment of that sort? Let the minister look through Tracy's accounts and see what the fruits of his policy are, and by its fruits ye shall know it. The minister will know whether they are bitter or sweet. Let him see what Tracy's accounts will bring forth. Why, it is impossible to imagine that that man meant to deal honestly with these people. What did Tracy want with thousands of tons of hay? This was hay that he got these Indians to put up, and in the fall he told them that he did not need it, and he paid them with

their own hay. Then the minister says: I will send up my law clerk to see if everything is all right. Mr. Williams goes up, and he conceives that he has done his whole duty if he sees that Tracy has kept his books rightly. He conceives, that so long as he finds that Tracy's and Funk's books show that the Indian was paid, it is all well and good. It does not matter how he was paid, it does not matter whether the mark on the back of the cheque is the Indian's or not; so long as the books are all right, everything is O.K., and the government is satisfied.

I cannot tell what was in Tracy's mind any more than I can tell what is in the minister's mind. But, I am not, unlike him, absolutely blind to the evidence:
Kappow Esqua, absent from the reserve, ascertained that he sold 32 acres for $80 to G. H. Funk.

That was $2.50 an acre. And there ends the report. And as soon as Mr. Williams found that out he did not think he should go and see this Indian at all wherever he was, but he reported, and that ended the

whole transaction. Two and a half dollars an acre for prime land in Manitoba. William Henderson, unable to see him, books of the purchaser, the Northwest Land Company show 68 acres bought for $220.

That was the extent of the investigation into this poor Indian's treatment. Oh, no, Mr. Williams went a step further; he looked up the books and he found that- the purchaser had a receipt from Andersons showing that the purchase price was $4 an acre all told, so that as soon as Investigate Williams found out that the poor Indian thought he was getting $5 down and the balance, he knew not what, when the patent issued, and that the purchaser's books showed that he sold for $4 all told, there the investigation closed. The report simply teems with cases of that sort. Here is the case of Mrs. David Prince, and it looks as though the sciuaws were not so businesslike as the Indians and did not fare so well. That ended it, neither in this case, nor in any other, did these investigators think it was any busi-Mr. MEIGHFN.

ness of theirs to take a look at the land and see whether it was worth $1.00 or $200 an acre. They did not care whether the land was sold for one-twentieth of its value or not, but they were deeply concerned to look at the books of the purchaser and take their statement for the facts. He claims he was to get at the time of sale $5 per acre and the balance when the department valued the land, but Mr. Williams had no corroboration, and he says he found acknowledgment for the above amount in full for the land. Let me suggest to the minister that whether it is right or whether it is not for the Department of Justice in Manitoba to investigate this case or any other case that has been suggested, the very same condition of affairs would confront them as confronted Mr. Williams-the poor Indian would be staked on the one hand and the speculator on the other, and where would be the Indian and where would be the prosecution? Let us take the case of William Starr. He sold 10 acres to William Kayner for $45, and 69 acres to George Tracy for $490. And the commissioner finds that there is a counter claim of $482, and that Starr disputed $64 of this, and he found that StaTr's contention was justified, but even so, that he was overpaid. Now, Mr. Speaker, here is a transaction, that the minister deems perfectly satisfactory, and still Mr. Williams found that this honest man, Mr. Tracy, had a false counter claim against him of $64, so false that even the Indian himself was believed, but because the purchaser's books showed him overpaid the whole thing is dropped. Such an investigation. Then, Mrs. Julia Stevenson sold 16 acres to W. D. Harper for $40, claimed that no price at all was mentioned and that she was entitled to $10 more, and that the purchaser had deeds signed and witnessed by her son. That is how they contrived to get that deed. They got the squaw to sign the deed and the Indian to witness it, and everything was all right. Then we have this report:
Consideration, $40. Has now paid $10 more to satisfy this old woman, and assumes a charge of $12 for improvement against the lot.

Fancy these poor people not knowing what they sold, hut in case of dispute, -taking a mere pittance from the purchaser; and these are the people whom the minister says are as competent to deal with land as are the members of this House. And these are the poor people that

the minister left complacently to their fate and literally threw into the jaws of the speculator. George Sanderson sold 98 acres, a nice sized farm, to George H. Funk for $500, and the report says he had no complaint at all, he also says that he sold 16 acres to a brother-in-law. Then there was the ease of Jessie Sanderson, and the commissioner says he was unable to see her, but the books of the purchaser, the Northwest Land Company, showed that 16 acres were bought for $50, or about- $3 an acre. And there was no investigation as to whether that land was worth $1 an acre or $50 an acre, but they could not see this poor squaw, and that was all they did about it. In the case of J ames Settee, he was absent from the reserve, but the report says that the books of the purchaser, the Northwest Land Company, showed 131 -60 acres bought for $400, or about $3 an acre. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, $3 an acre for prime farm land 25 miles from Winnipeg. It is all very well for the hon. member for Provencher, or for the Minister of the Interior, to talk to parties in this House who do not know anything about values of western lands; but those of us who have lived there are not children. Does the Minitser of the Interior imagine for a moment that land within 25 miles-of the city of Winnipeg, on the line of an electric railway, and admittedly good land -not sand, not swamp, not alkali, not even scrub-is worth only $3 an acre, or even five times $3-nay, seven times $3 an acre? There is no land in Manitoba that can be placed in that position, and the Minister of the Interior knows it as well as I do. Tell the people of Selkirk or the people of Winnipeg that good land, well situated on the river bank, is worth, only $20 an acre even. It would be ridiculously cheao at $20 an acre; it would- be cheap at $30 an acre. I challenge any member from western Canada to say that that statement is not true.

These are the fruits of the course deliberately adopted by this department, with the result of making the Indians drunk, and the
speculators rich. These are the fruits of the course they adopted, and in regard to which they put between themselves, and harm the robes of Chief Justice Howell.

There is certainly an important issue at stake in this matter. If this House votes nay to the resolution of the hon. member for Selkirk, it votes approval of that manner of treating the wards of this country. PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,I live in a town that has a considerably larger population, and I have no doubt that if it were made a customs outport the collections there would be five times, perhaps ten times, as much as they would be in Elora; yet

we have not a building there, either for a post office, or a custom house. I would like to know what grounds the people of Elora expect that the Minister of Customs will make it an outport. I do not know of any industrial institutions there that would require imports of any great extent. I understand that the policy of the Minister of Customs is to open outports, not for the convenience of the people, but for the collection of revenue. I do not see why the minister should erect a building for an outport at Elora, when his colleague does not approve of opening more customs outports. There have been very few customs ports opened by the present government. When the late govern-mejit went out of power, I think there were only 45 customs ports in Ontario. Now there are 52, and probably'seven or eight of the increases are caused by raising outports to ports. PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,I am glad to hear the minister speak about erecting cheaper buildings in small towns, because unless a policy of that kind is adopted, we can never hope to get public buildings in towns ranging from 1,500 up to 2,500 of a population. Years ago I commended that policy to the Hon. Mr. Tarte, when he was Minister of Public Works, and he did undertake to. carry that policy into effect. He started with the town of Clinton, with the idea of erecting a building for a post office that-would cost under $10,000. Building was cheaper in those days than it is at the present time. But I was informed, I think by the member of the county at that time, Mr. Holmes, that the chief architect told him that they would not draw plans for a building to cost less than $10,000. Mr. Tarte attempted to get a cheaper building, and I remember that before it was completed the cost went up to $15,000. Now, the minister will require to exercise a great deal of care, otherwise this $12,000 will likely Teach $20,000 before the building is completed. His officers will require to keep a close watch, and if the.y do so, I Mr. BLAIN.

think the cost can be kept down. But there is a danger that the officers of the government will give greater latitude, and that the whole purpose of the minister will fail. His purpose is a good one, I approve of it. It is oniy by erecting cheaper buildings that we can hope to have more of them. A good building to-day can be erected no doubt for $15,000 as a post office; yes, and for less, giving ample ac-, commodation, for any town the size of Elora and Fergus, with all the fittings required. The minister, in answer to the hon. member for East Toronto, stated that in Elora an additional official would be required as a caretaker. I do not think that should be the policy of the minister. The postmaster, I think, ought to be responsible for the care of that building. In erecting a building the minister should provide a residence for the postmaster as well as the post office. Let the postmaster live in the same building and be the caretaker of the building, and thereby save considerable expense. When Mr. Tarte decided to erect the building in Clinton I understood that that was the policy, that he was going to make it a residence for the postmaster as well as a post office. That is a policy the present minister mighu adopt with a areat deal of advantage. The use of the building^ as a residence would be ample compensation for looking after it.

PETER'S INDIAN RESERVE.,,,I do not have that information, because the postmaster at present is paid on the revenue basis, by a percentage of the receipts, and if he has an assistant, that assistant would be paid by himself, and not by the department. The only additional officer that will be required here is The caretaker. _ Of course there is a good deal to be said in favour of the policy advocated by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), but there is a good deal to be said the other way. If the policy were generally adopted of erecting post offices in such a manner as to provide a residence for the postmaster, it would mean a good deal of additional expense. The postmaster is quite an important man in a town, and he would want a good deal better residence than would be suitable for the caretaker. It would mean having larger rooms, and a greater number. Our experience has not been that providing a residence for a postmaster in a public building has resulted in a saving to the public.

But I wish to say that there are many places throughout the country, with a population almost as great as these two, towns, where the post office is in a part of the residence of the postmaster himself, and where the revenue runs from $700 up to $1,000 or over. Now, I do not think it is fair to expend $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 in erecting post offices in comparatively small villages such as these, while there are a great many rural sections where the people have a mail service only twice or three times a week, or perhaps where they have no service at all, and have to go several miles for their mail.
